en: The Scripture of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Part One:
The Introductory Chapter. Chapter One: The Introduction.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Bhagavān was staying at the Bodhi tree in the country of Magadha, at the Vajra Seat,
within a great precious canopy, the place where he had attained perfect enlightenment.
The jeweled pavilion on that ground, manifested by the Tathāgata, was perfectly adorned and pure;
it was entirely composed of immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous rarities,
variously embellished and spontaneously manifest.
Various colors interreflect, emitting a great radiance;
a wondrous jewel-wheel is pure and perfect,
adorned with the intermingling of immeasurable hues.
It manifested throughout the entire site,
with various wonderful and multicolored jeweled canopies,
and banners and pennants whose radiance shone brilliantly.
A network of seven precious jewels, adorned with exquisite fragrant flower tassels,
covers it entirely. It rains down all manner of infinite great treasures,
and various precious trees appear spontaneously.
The branches and leaves were lush and radiant, and the filaments of the flowers emitted wondrous fragrances.
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, this site was made vast,
majestic, and pure, with light shining everywhere.
A mass of all manner of rare and wondrous jewels;
an altar site adorned with immeasurable roots of goodness;
and a Bodhi tree that was lofty, prominent, and extraordinary.
With lapis lazuli for its trunk and exquisite jewels for its branches,
precious leaves hang down like layered clouds,
while flowers of various jewel colors are interspersed throughout.
Great precious maṇi-jewels serve as its fruit.
The radiance of these trees illuminates all buddha-fields,
manifesting various transformations to perform the work of a Buddha.
This is the Bodhisattva Teaching on the Most Sublime Chapter of the Mantra of the Universal Manifestation of the Mahāyāna One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin.
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he produced various kinds of sublime Brahma-sounds.
He praised the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata’s One-Syllable Vidyā, the Uṣṇīṣarāja.
His lion throne was composed of vajra,
lofty, vast, and exquisitely beautiful.
A king of maṇi jewels forms its pedestal,
adorned with a variegated array of all kinds of precious flowers and wondrous gems,
and covered above by a net of pearls.
The flowing radiance from the various jeweled ornaments was like clouds,
illuminating the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and manifesting the teachings of the Tathāgata’s skillful means.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon this seat,
having attained supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena,
and knowing and seeing that the three periods of time are entirely equal.
His body was resplendent, emitting the light of immeasurable koṭis of sun-discs as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
illuminating all the oceans of lands and the sites of enlightenment of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, which are boundless and limitless.
Within the radiance of each respective site of enlightenment,
he expounded the teachings on all dharmas of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King,
guiding, transforming, and subduing all sentient beings.
The light pervades the ten directions, reaching every place without exception.
All the supernatural transformations of all Buddhas of the past, present,
and future are fully visible within that radiance.
All the inconceivable matters of all Buddha-lands,
including every form of adornment, were likewise manifested.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats.
He is well-able to tame himself and cast off all heavy burdens;
having exhausted the fetters of the outflows, he is no longer subject to afflictions.
His aggregate of morality is pure and white, his mind is purified, and he possesses liberation and the purity of wisdom through liberation.
Having well cultivated the Buddha-wisdom and completed what was to be done,
they have attained great mastery and fully realized their own benefit;
having reached the other shore, their fame is heard everywhere.

Their names were: the Venerable Śāriputra; the Venerable Kāśyapa; the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa; the Venerable Gayākāśyapa; the Venerable Mahākāśyapa; the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana; the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; the Venerable Subhadra; the Venerable Upānanda; the Venerable Bāṣpika; the Venerable Aniruddha; the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra; the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila; the Venerable Gavāmpati; the Venerable Mahāgavāmpati; the Venerable Sunakṣatra; the Venerable Mahāsunakṣatra; the Venerable Subhūti; the Venerable Kauṇḍinya; the Venerable Caityagandhara; the Venerable Rāhula; and the Venerable Ānanda.
Thus, he was accompanied by such a great assembly of śrāvakas.
Furthermore, there were countless great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had all achieved the various pāramitās;
their ocean of merit was profound, vast, and boundless.
The Tathāgata’s practice-ground, his aspiration for omniscience, and his profound and secret teachings are all fully perfected.
He thoroughly knows all the conduct of sentient beings and,
by means of vajra-wisdom, teaches the Dharma as is appropriate.
Skillfully entering the great ocean of all dharmas that constitute the merits of all Tathāgatas,
they saturate their own bodies and travel throughout the ocean-like assemblies of all Buddha-fields,
paying homage to and making offerings to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
He has thoroughly penetrated the great ocean of dhāraṇīs, wisdom, and eloquence of all the stages,
as well as the immeasurable and boundless samādhi-doors for manifesting supernatural powers and transformations.
Unimpeded and uniquely penetrating,
his name was the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajradhvaja.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secret Traces.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrasārāśaya,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dṛḍhāśaya,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganāmala.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalamati,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayamati.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Trailokyasamatikrānta,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anabhibhūtadhara.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Viśvabhū,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Devamukuṭa,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candraprabha Kumāra,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Acintyamatī,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahājava,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnaśikhin,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Supratabhuja.
He was accompanied by such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these,
as well as by immeasurable and innumerable deva-kings from the three thousandfold world system,
namely, Śakra-devānām-indra, the king of the gods.
Mahābrahmā Deva-rāja,
Yama Dharmarāja,
and Varuṇa Deva-rāja.
The Deva King Vāyu,
the Deva King Vaiśravaṇa,
and the Deva King Sūbhūma.
The Great Lord King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations,
the King Nārāyaṇa, and the King Īśāna.
In this manner, it extends even to the devaputras of Radiant Flames,
the devaputras of Vast Fruit,
and the devaputras of the Pure Abodes.
Together with such celestial kings as these,
those of great majesty and their retinues,
there were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great accomplished mantra-seers (vidyādhara-rṣis).
These are the vidyādhara-siddhas of the wheel-mantra,
the vidyādhara-siddhas of the sword-mantra,
and the vidyādhara-siddhas of the vajra-mantra.
The accomplished mantra-siddha of the Lotus family;
the accomplished mantra-siddha of the Battle-axe family;
the accomplished mantra-siddha of the Tathāgata lineage’s Great Radiant Mantra; and the accomplished mantra-siddha of the Lotus lineage.
Vidyādharas who have accomplished the Vajra family;
vidyādharas who have accomplished Maheśvara;
vidyādharas who have accomplished Nārāyaṇa.
They are accomplished mantra-adepts of the yakṣī lineage;
they are accomplished mantra-adepts of the mahoraga class;
they are accomplished mantra-adepts of the garuḍa class.
Siddhas who have accomplished the spells of nāgas;
siddhas who have accomplished the spells of ḍākinīs;
and siddhas who have accomplished the spells of yakṣas.
He accomplished the vidyādhara-rishis Ratnabhadra and Pūrṇabhadra;
he accomplished the vidyādhara-rishi Vaiśravaṇa;
and he accomplished the vidyādhara-rishi Varuṇa.
Accompanied by accomplished mantra-vidyādhara sages such as these,
with those of great majestic power as their leaders.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of mantra-king messengers from the Tathāgata family,
mantra-king messengers from the Lotus family,
and mantra-king messengers from the Maṇi family.
The Vajra-clan mantra-king messengers,
together with such a host of mantra-king messengers,
were accompanied by those of great majestic power as their leaders.
Furthermore, there are all the supramundane and mundane deities of stupas,
the deities of the Dharma,
and the deities of space.
The deity of flowers and fruits, the deity of flavors,

the deity of crops, the mountain deity, the ocean deity, the river deity, the island deity, the city deity, the town deity, the house deity, the street deity, the lane deity, the tree deity, the forest deity, the *śītavana* (cemetery) deity, and the palace deity.
He was accompanied by such great divine kings as these,
with those of great majestic virtue as their leaders;
furthermore, there were ten billion sun deities, moon deities, and stellar deities.
The celestial lords and others,
led by those of great majesty and power,
were present together with all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and asuras.
Garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, piśāca ghosts,
bhūta ghosts, and the mātṛkā goddesses such as Hārītī—
those of great majesty and power were present together as their leaders.
Furthermore, there was the ghost-king Nandīśvara as their leader,
accompanied by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of ghosts;
and there was also the celestial king Maheśvara as their leader, accompanied [by his own assembly].
He presides over an immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *jvara* demons as his retinue.
Furthermore, together with the *kumbhāṇḍa* king *Carcikā* as his leader,
he presides over an immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *kumbhāṇḍa* demons as his retinue.
Within that assembly,
there were also immeasurable devas and sons of devas from other directions,
as well as asuras and sons of asuras.
The great Vināyakas and others,
led by those of great majesty and power,
were present together in this trichiliocosm.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, all the devas, great mantra-vidyādharas, nāgas, spirits,
and ghosts [gathered] within a circumference of five hundred yojanas around the site of the Bodhi tree.
Having gathered together as a great assembly,
they sat in the hall without harming or vexing one another.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya.
And he addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:
"Good sons, this tree is the Tree Adorned by All Bodhi.
When I first sat beneath this tree..."
"Then, having destroyed the four māras, you shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
You all should likewise sit upon this ground,
so that you may realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of all buddhas."
Having spoken these words, he became silent and motionless.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secret Traces,
through the Buddha’s majestic power and by virtue of the power of his original vows from the past, [arose].
Immediately rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder,
adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined,
and gazing up at the World-Honored One with reverence, addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One."
I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
regarding the mantra-teaching of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin:
by what skillful means can one achieve results with little effort?
One immediately attains the accomplishment of the Sovereign Wheel-King of the Single-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa of all Tathāgatas—
the most supreme vidyā-mantra dharma that is unimpeded in both the supramundane and mundane realms—
along with the methods for painting its image and the rules for ritual bathing.
Entering samādhi through the preparatory rites, seals, and mandalas;
the methods for superior, middling, and inferior accomplishments;
and the methods for sitting, reclining, reciting, and maintaining [the practice].
The secret and profound method for binding the wheel-mudrā;
the method for realizing supernormal powers; the method for eliminating karmic obstructions;
the method for great peace and security; the method for great abundance; and the method for subduing māras and enemies.
The true dharmas of the mantras of all Tathāgata families;
the rite of self-consecration; the rite of the homa altar;
the rites for various times; and the rites for selecting the site.
Extending thus extensively to all sentient beings and the entire realm of sentient beings,
the Bodhisattva accomplishes the dhāraṇī-mantra methods of practice,
causing all sentient beings within the realm of Jambudvīpa to attain great peace and happiness.
By the power of the mantra of the Tathāgata One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin,
all these sentient beings shall perform great Buddha-activities.
By this cause and condition, [this shall come to pass].
All sentient beings within the realm of Jambudvīpa shall attain great peace and happiness;
they will be able to accomplish the Dharma of the Cakravartin King of Uṣṇīṣas,
as well as achieve all the mantra-dharmas of the devas and all lineages of celestial deities.
The incantation methods for all nāgas and all nāga lineages;
the incantation methods for all yakṣas and all yakṣa lineages;
the incantation methods for all rākṣasas and all rākṣasa lineages.
All gandharvas and all lineages of gandharvas and their incantation methods;
all asuras and all lineages of asuras and their incantation methods.
The incantation methods for all garuḍas and all garuḍa lineages;
the incantation methods for all kiṃnaras and all kiṃnara lineages.
All the mantras and ritual methods of all the mahoragas and all their lineages,
as well as all mundane and supramundane dharmas,
shall be fully accomplished without any hindrance.
To serve as a great place of refuge for all sentient beings,
may you eliminate all defilements and obstacles to accomplish my dhāraṇī methods,
as well as the seal-mandala and dhāraṇī methods of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and other bodhisattvas of great majestic power.
And because it is the locus for accomplishing the immeasurable varieties of seal-mandalas (*mudrā-maṇḍala*) and mantra-rites taught by all Tathāgatas, which are otherwise difficult to accomplish;
we pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, [will grant his grace].
"Out of compassion, guide sentient beings by expounding this for our sake.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Lord of Secrets!"
"You shall be able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings of the future.
Regarding my question concerning this single-syllable *Buddhoṣṇīṣacakravartin*, the supreme chapter,
which accomplishes all mantra-circles, rituals, and so forth spoken by all Tathāgatas."
It causes all mantra-practitioners to abide in the path of diligent cultivation.
Therefore, Guhyapati, you should listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well and retain it.
I shall now, for your sake, analyze and explain the supreme Dharma-mother of all Tathāgatas, the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin.
It causes all sons of the Buddha to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.
I see that all Tathāgatas of the past have already spoken it,
and all Tathāgatas of the future shall speak it.
I, as well as all the Tathāgatas currently residing in the lands of the ten directions, now speak.

At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—[spoke thus].
Then, with the Buddha-eye,
he observed exhaustively and completely all buddha-fields, all sentient beings, and the realm of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, across the past, present, and future.
And regarding all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm,
at each of the locations where they previously cultivated roots of goodness through the power of causal vows,
he addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:
Noble son, remember the mantra of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin of all Tathāgatas,
the supreme great samādhi,
the locus of most inconceivable supernormal powers.
This Dharma is able to perform great Buddha-works in all worlds.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
having received the Buddha’s instruction, each contemplated the method of the Samādhi of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakra-Rāja.
Except for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secret Traces.
Why? Because of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat beneath the Bodhi tree on the ground of adamantine merit.
He then entered the Great Samādhi of the Miraculous Transformation of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakra-Rāja of All Tathāgatas.
Simultaneously, all Tathāgatas in all present lands throughout the ten directions [assembled].
They all sat beneath bodhi trees on adamantine grounds of merit,
and each likewise entered the samādhi of the miraculous transformations of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, when the World-Honored One entered this samādhi of spiritual transformation,
he fully and completely recollected all buddha-fields and all sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
And regarding all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm,
he has accumulated [merit] over immeasurable koṭis of Ganges-sand-like great kalpas through his cultivation.

From the thirty-two marks of a great man, he radiates great light from the boundless roots of goodness consisting of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, ascetic practices, and other virtues.
That is to say: the crown of the head, the hair-tuft between the eyebrows, the eyes, ears, nose, temples, cheeks,
lips, mouth, teeth, gums, palate, jaw, shoulders, elbows,
arms, hands, chest, breasts, heart, navel, and the *svastika* mark upon the chest.
The thighs, knees, shins, ankles, wrists, palms, backs of the hands,
and fingers [constitute] the Tathāgata’s Dharma-seal of the thousand-spoked wheel,
the Tathāgata’s wish-fulfilling seal, and the Tathāgata’s spear seal.
The Tathāgata’s staff seal, the Tathāgata’s heart seal,
the Tathāgata’s invincible wrathful Uṣṇīṣacakravartin samādhi’s invincible seal,
the Tathāgata’s great loving-kindness, and the Tathāgata’s great compassion.
The Tathāgata’s samādhi, the Tathāgata’s fearlessness,
the bestowing of predictions upon the assembly, and the Tathāgata’s great vidyā-mantra king—
each of these characteristics emitted immeasurable varieties of light.
Each of those lights was adorned by a surrounding array of various kinds of radiance;
from the very crown of his head, he emitted immeasurable, innumerable, extraordinary, and most excellent hundreds of thousands of rays of light.
Each of those lights possesses various mixed colors—
namely, blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and variegated light.
These lights blaze brilliantly, illuminating throughout the immeasurable and innumerable diverse Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
Furthermore, all hells and animal realms within this trichiliocosm, as well as all sentient beings of dark karma,
shall have all their sins and afflictions completely extinguished.
All the Bodhisattvas who practice the transformation of all conditioned phenomena through the holding of mantras shall achieve complete accomplishment upon encountering this light.
Such manifestations as these are entirely the immeasurable and vast merit of the Tathāgata.
The light shines with nourishing moisture, manifesting the inconceivable;
in a mere moment, it brings about great benefit and happiness,
uprooting all the karma of suffering for all sentient beings.
The light shines forth, eclipsing all Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
as well as all the realms of Māra, the palaces of Māra, and the radiance of Māra;
it completely illuminates all such worlds.
From the peak of existence above down to the Avīci Hell below,
whatever sentient beings encountered this light were each comforted and reassured,
their bodies and minds filled with joy.
The light returned and circled the Buddha three times,
each resuming its original form.
At that time, after Śākyamuni Tathāgata had emitted this light, [he remained silent].
Rising slowly and calmly from samādhi,
he surveyed the various buddha-fields and the assembled multitude. Then,
like a lion king, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi Guhyapati, saying:
Listen now attentively to the Great Vidyārāja-mantra of the One-Syllable Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin,
the Vidyārāja-mantra of Buddhalocanā,
and the Vidyārāja-mantra of the Four Vajraśṛṅkhalās.
These kings of mantras are the hands of the Tathāgata;
they are the lips of the Tathāgata; they are the wheel-turning kings of the mouth of the Tathāgata, bestowing great benefit and liberation upon all sentient beings.
If all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in this world,
as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all sons and daughters of noble family, [should hear this...]
For one who is fully able to rely on the Dharma and thus recite, study, and uphold this One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin Great Mantra,
all the various gods, worldlings, spirits, and ghosts will [be unable to harm them].
None shall be able to harm or cause destruction;
this person shall attain all peace and longevity,
immeasurable merit and happiness, and practice great compassion.
Abiding on the stage of non-retrogression, they are free from all afflictions and ailments;
fire cannot harm them, water cannot drown them, and weapons cannot cause untimely injury.
Neither poisons nor venomous snakes can inflict harm upon them.
This single-syllable mantra of mine, the King of the Uṣṇīṣa Samādhi, is produced from this:
if there are newly initiated Mahāyāna bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and other such persons, [who recite it...]
Those who believe in, recite, uphold, transcribe,
or wear [this] shall attain peace and security;
they will be constantly protected by all the immeasurable devas of great majesty and virtue.
No evil devas, nāgas, or vināyakas shall obstruct or afflict them.
One who copies this [text] should bathe cleanly and wear fresh, pure garments.
Having observed the ritual fast according to the Dharma and sitting by the side of the altar,
one should write the mantra with realgar on birch bark and bestow it upon the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
One should place it in the corner of one's *kāṣāya* robe and wear it with reverence.
If there are kings, members of the royal clan, queens, consorts, ministers, officials, or sons and daughters of noble families who wish to wear it, they may do so.
If one wears it upon the head, fastens it around the neck,
or places it upon the wrist or arm, one will attain peace and security,
being freed from all obstacles, afflictions, malevolent spirits, calamities, and diseases.
He shall always be observed, honored, and praised by the devas;
he shall not fall into the realms of the various evil destinies.
Guhyapati is the great king of mantras.
It can also extinguish all calamitous stars and strange portents, bringing about great peace and happiness;
it can also subdue all devas, nāgas, the eight classes of supernatural beings, gods, and ghosts;
and it can accomplish the unsurpassed karmic conditions for those who recite this mantra.
Again, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of the Secret Traces, saying:
"This is the mantra of the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa Cakra-rāja of all Tathāgatas;
it is the mantra of the High-Crested Uṣṇīṣa Cakra-rāja."
The Mantra of the Victorious Crown King (Jin-ding-lun-wang) and the Mantra of the Radiant Mass Crown King (Guang-zu-ding-lun-wang) both abide equally within the samādhi of all Tathāgatas.
Although their supernatural powers are all equal, immeasurable, and vast,
they still cannot equal the power of the supreme great samādhi vidyā-mantra of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin.
For what reason is this mantra supreme and peerless?
It is, for example, like the Buddha-Eye Illuminating Mantra or the Buddha-Urṇā-Keśa Mantra.
The mantra of the King of the Destroying Uṣṇīṣa and the mantra of the Invincible Wrathful King—
these mantras are spoken together.
For these reasons, he is named the Peerless One, the Supreme Equal of the Unequaled.
Furthermore, from his Great Compassion, this Great Man utters the Great Lion’s Roar,
which none of the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas can ever destroy.
The supernatural powers, majestic virtue, and auspicious protection of all Buddhas bestow their empowerment.
They produce the great light of wisdom to shatter all darkness;
with firm, profound, and pure insight, they manifest auspicious signs of merit and majesty, most supreme in the world.
Stainless, pure, courageous, and firm,

he manifests the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges that bring about liberation from birth, the knowledge of the four foundations of mindfulness, and the knowledge of non-forgetfulness— vast and immeasurable.
It can produce the great radiant majesty of the ten powers of the adamantine *anantara*,
extinguishing all defilements and obstructions to enter the wisdom of all Buddhas;
it can produce all the meritorious virtues of the myriad practices of the great Bodhisattvas, as well as the marks and signs of a Tathāgata and the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*).
He is the one capable of performing all courageous and tranquil dharmas, the banner of the Dharma, the lofty and unobstructed locus of great majesty,
and the source of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity that provides the noble truths as a path for all sentient beings with evil karma.
This is the samādhi of the Great Mirror-like Wisdom of Unsurpassed Bodhi, which can manifest the spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to manifest the great majestic power of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakra King, [spoke as follows].
Suddenly his physical form transformed into that of a great universal monarch (cakravartin),

From each of the treasures, a great wheel of light was emitted, illuminating the boundless.
All the jewels of the Dharma appeared simultaneously,
emitting a variegated radiance of gems;

His physical form was resplendent, emitting various kinds of light that illuminated all things like a mass of molten gold.
He then spoke the One-Syllable Buddhōṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin Dhāraṇī, saying:

*Namo* (the first character pronounced *na-nai-ge*, hereafter the same; the second character pronounced *mo-zie-su-ge*, hereafter the same) *Mantradā* (the first character pronounced *man-duo-tuo-ke*, hereafter the same) *Buddhānām* (1) *Oṃ* (2) *Hūṃ* (3) *Bhṛṅgiṇi* (4) *Hūṃ*. At that time, when the Tathāgata spoke this mantra, [the earth shook in six ways].
The trichiliocosm, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
shook six times simultaneously,
like the violent winds of the whirlwind in Jambudvīpa.
It blew through the various groves, causing the grasses and trees to tremble;
within this, all the Sumeru Kings likewise shook violently,
and all rivers and oceans surged and boiled.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, great fires broke out everywhere throughout all the palaces of the Māras.
Therein, the various Māras, oppressed by the fire,
were all struck with terror and cried out, taking refuge in the Buddha.
All the sufferings of the hells were extinguished;
among those sentient beings in the assembly, including their respective retinues,
there was not a single one who could even look up at him.
This assembly consisted entirely of great bodhisattvas such as Maitreya and others,
none of whom were able even to look upon him.
Among them were the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, in an instant, he became dazed and collapsed to the ground.
At that time, those gods of great majesty and virtue—
namely Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, Śakra Devendra, Kubera, Varuṇa, and Yama, the Dharma King— [all arrived].
Even all the devas and celestial deities, and all the spirits and ghosts of great majesty,
dropped the wheels, halberds, vajras, nooses, and tridents they held,
as well as the various implements in the hands of their respective attendants. All these weapons fell away completely.
By the power of the Buddha’s empowerment,
these bodhisattvas recollected the great samādhi of the bodhi-superpowers of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin of all Tathāgatas.

and attain a power equal to that of the One-Syllable Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin Dhāraṇī.
Why is this? Because it is sustained by the power of the samādhis and other qualities of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets, saying:
"I shall now again enter the Great Samādhi of the Inconceivable Supernatural Powers of All Tathāgatas."

He clearly proclaimed the mantra of the Supreme Wheel King (*Paramādhirāja*), its supernatural powers and majestic virtue, for the sake of extinguishing all manner of sufferings of sentient beings in the evil destinies and hells; and in order to manifest the supernatural powers and majestic virtue of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, he entered the Great Inconceivable Great Samādhi and spoke this mantra: [Mantra follows]
*Namo samantabuddhānām | Oṃ hūṃ jvala jyotir-ṣṇiṣe jvala jvala bandha bandha namaḥ namaḥ nṛmuṇḍa haṃ haḥ haṃ hūṃ.* While this mantra was being spoken, this great trichiliocosm...
Furthermore, all the Buddha-fields shook in six great ways;
through the Buddha’s majestic power, this miraculous transformation was manifested,
yet no sentient beings were at all terrified.
May the various intense sufferings of all sentient beings in the hells be completely stilled;
may all those hungry ghosts simultaneously obtain satiation with sweet and delicious food.

Guhya-pati, this mantra of the Supreme Cakravartin King was expounded through the miraculous transformations of the supernatural powers of as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
Guhya-pati, it was taught for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings who are afraid; wherever this mantra resides, [there shall be safety].
If one merely observes or reads it for a moment,
all māras will not enter therein;
how much more so for one who upholds it!
If there is a son of good family who, day and night, diligently recites, studies,
and upholds this Supreme Cakravartin King Mantra,
before long he shall attain the inconceivable realm of supernormal powers, miraculous transformations, and the gateways of samādhi.
They are venerated and honored by devas and humans,
and they attain a body that is an inconceivable mass of merit.
If there are those with sincere faith who study the Mahāyāna, [they shall likewise attain this].
Furthermore, if one can have faith in and incline toward this *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin-vijaya-pada*,
and is able to constantly and sincerely recite, read, and uphold it,
one shall swiftly realize the profound, inconceivable, and equal supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of all Tathāgatas, as well as the supreme wisdom-samādhi of supernatural power.
Surpassing all sentient beings in merit, longevity, prosperity, and excellence,
they shall have their every wish fulfilled and be honored by others.
Lord of Secret Traces, such is the result for one who thus diligently upholds this Sovereign Wheel-King Mantra of the Supreme Crown.
Before long, this person will also attain supernormal powers (abhijñā).
All celestial Māras, Vināyakas, malevolent spirits, ghosts,
and the like will not approach them at all.
If one encounters such a person, they will all be terrified and flee, losing their great majestic power.
Guhyapati, if a person believes in, practices, and realizes this mantra,
it is identical to realizing the one-syllable Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin vidyā-mantra chapter.
One is able to give rise to supernormal powers and enter the hells to deliver all sentient beings from the suffering of their transgressions.
Lord Guhyapati, this mantra possesses immeasurable and boundless merit and supernormal powers.
I have now briefly described but a small portion of it.
Even if I were to praise these merits extensively for immeasurable eons, I could not exhaust them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:
Noble son, these mantra syllables of the Five-Crested Wheel-King King emerged and manifested from the Great Samādhi of the supernatural power and majesty of all Tathāgatas.
Even if I were to spend hundreds of thousands of koṭis of great eons speaking of the supernatural powers and merits of these mantras, I could not exhaust them.
For now, I have merely spoken briefly for the sake of benefiting and liberating all sentient beings.

Even if the Tathāgata were to remain for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of great kalpas and speak the mantras of the Five-Crested Wheel-Turning Kings and their lineages, he could not exhaustively reach the limits of each individual mantra of these five families.
Guhya-pati, if there is a son of good family who dwells in the presence of immeasurable Buddha-Bhagavāns and offers them superior robes,
bedding, medicinal requisites, food and drink, wealth, treasures, and all such things;
If one were to offer sustenance and perform worship three times every day for a hundred thousand kalpas,
the merit thereby obtained would be but a hundred-thousand-millionth part [of the merit gained by this practice].

It is not equal to the merit of someone who, for twenty-one days, maintains these supreme vidyā-mantra syllables of the Five-Crested Wheel-Turning King (Pañcaśīrṣa-cakravartin) according to the Dharma. Why is this?
Because those who read, recite, receive, and maintain these supreme vidyā-mantra syllables of the Five-Crested Wheel-Turning King shall attain accomplishment.
This person will certainly attain the stage of an irreversible Bodhisattva.
Their physical marks and majestic virtue will be extraordinary within the three realms.
With firm and steadfast vigor, they shall transcend birth, aging, and death.
Śakra, Lord of the Desire Realm, and all the gods of great majesty and virtue,
upon seeing this person who has accomplished the Five-Peaked Cakravartin Mantra,
shall rise from their seats to welcome and honor them.
Their heads were split into seven pieces like the branches of an *ari* tree.
The radiance, majestic virtue, and supernatural power of the bodies of Maheśvara, Śakra Devendra, Nārāyaṇa, Vaiśravaṇa, and all the other devas [were likewise eclipsed].
All those who have been certified as practitioners of the mantra of this Five-Crested Wheel-Turning King are eclipsed by his radiance and majestic virtue so that they no longer appear.
This person’s majestic light constantly shines with such brilliance that it surpasses that of all the devas by hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of times.
Furthermore, there may be individuals of great merit and purely virtuous character who,
with faith, aspiration, and a sincere intention, have accomplished this mantra;
such persons should transcribe this sutra according to the Dharma, and read, recite, and uphold it.
They shall constantly make offerings with ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flowers, fruits, food, and drink.
If such persons see those who have faith in the Buddha’s supernormal powers, the ten powers, his majestic virtue, and all profound dharmas, and who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle;
Then one should explain it for them; by not harboring stinginess or parsimony, they will immediately attain success.
For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they shall not fall into hell and shall obtain the knowledge of past lives.
Until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
they shall always be observed, revered, and protected by all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings;
and no māras whatsoever shall disturb or harm them.
All those taught by him receive his instructions with reverence.
When his life comes to an end, it is as if he were entering meditative absorption.
Guhyapati, there are sons of good family who...
Of noble lineage, with true and excellent parents, born under an auspicious constellation;
endowed with all sense faculties, his body is beautiful and handsome;
his complexion is ruddy white, and his bones and joints do not protrude.
His arms and hands are smooth and slender, neither too short nor coarse;
he is neither too stout nor too thin, and his fingernails are crimson.
His feet possess the mark of the deer-king, and both his ankles are flat and full.
The teeth are neither sparse nor protruding, nor are they yellow or black; they are bright white, even, and closely set.
The eyes do not squint or look askance, nor are they clouded by cataracts or colored yellow or green.
The nose is not flat or crooked, and the lips are neither cleft nor shriveled.
The face is neither sunken nor narrow, and the skin is radiant and smooth;
one suffers neither from scabies, leprosy, rheumatism, nor eczema,
and does not crave sensual desires.
They shall not be disturbed or harassed by vināyakas;
their merit and wisdom will be pure and perfect;
and by their very nature, they will take refuge in the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
They do not believe in or serve various heavens, celestial deities, heterodox spirits, or ghosts;
they are constantly diligent without indolence, restraining their minds with vigor, and delighting solely in the cultivation and study of the Mahāyāna teachings.
Desiring to fulfill the great vows of a bodhisattva,
to transcend all demonic realms, and to advance toward the bodhisattva stages—
such a person is worthy of receiving this sutra and achieving this mantra.
Guhya-pati, if you see such a person, you should regard them as a virtuous friend and,
by means of various skillful methods, teach them this mantra, its merits, and the instructions for its practice.
You should cause this person to swiftly attain the ground of the supreme and victorious dharma of this Great Pañcamudrā-cakravartin.
Guhya-pati, this King of Mantras is difficult to see or hear in immeasurable Buddha-fields.
Those who are able to hear it have all been blessed by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
If one obtains this sutra, one is then a member of the Tathāgata’s lineage and kin.
Why is this? Because this Tathāgata-mantra, the King of Samādhis, is truly inconceivable.
Among all mantras, this is the most supreme, the most excellent, the great and foremost.
Sentient beings such as these should resolutely give rise to the highest resolve and accomplish this Pañcaśīrṣa Cakravartin Mantra.
If there are sentient beings who seek this sutra and,
being pure and in accordance with the Dharma,
either transcribe it or recite this mantra and this sutra;
It should be known that such a person shall immediately attain this King of Samādhis of the Five-Crested Wheel-Turning King Mantra,
forever severing the flow of craving, the thieves of the fetters of ignorance, and the stubborn, dull-witted minds of hatred, delusion, and malice.
This is because he is revered, honored, and relied upon by all the devas.
Chapter Two: The Ritual for Painting Images from the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin-tantra*. At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni again surveyed the assembly with his Buddha-eye.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi Guhyapati, saying:
"Good son, listen once more attentively. This image of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin has been proclaimed by immeasurable koṭis of Ganges-sand-like Buddhas in common."
Among all the manifestations of the supramundane and mundane worlds, this image is the most supreme;
it benefits all sentient beings burdened by obstacles and afflictions.
This image is, indeed, the miraculous transformation of the supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas.
Adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, wearing crowns, ribbons, and robes,
he delivers all sentient beings burdened by the defilements of sin,
leading them to the shore of nirvana through the Samādhi of the Supreme.

The one who paints this image must have previously entered the unsurpassed empowerment mandala of this Cakravartin King and received from the hands of the ācārya the complete mantras, mudrās, and rituals.
Alternatively, having entered the Maṇḍala of the Supreme Crown King (*Vijayacūḍarāja*) and attained accomplishment,
one is authorized by the seal of the *ācārya*’s praise; thus,
one seeks to realize the state of supramundane great *nirvāṇa*.
A practitioner such as this is fit to paint the image.
One should commission a brahmin of pure conduct who is a faithful believer,
or a young girl of noble lineage whose parents are truly and faithfully devoted.
Instruct them to purify and maintain [the materials].
When spinning, processing, weaving, or sewing, do not use coarse or inferior thread; blend and weave it properly for painting.
Do not cut it with a knife.
The width shall be four cubits and the length six cubits;
alternatively, the width may be three cubits and the length five cubits.
If one lacks the strength to weave it in such proportions, [one may adjust accordingly].
Furthermore, one may purchase fresh, clean, and high-quality items at one's own discretion;
do not bargain over the price.
Once the items have been acquired, bathe them according to the Dharma using pure scented water.
Then, for the central painting:
the pigments should be fresh and pure; do not use hide glue or water to mix the colors.
Instead, use fragrant glue to blend the pigments for the painting.
Alternatively, one may take the rules of procedure from the teachings within the lineage of the Tathāgata;
it is also permissible to use a painted image.
As for the one who paints this image:
One should adorn and decorate [the altar] with the supernatural powers of all Buddhas during the months of the first,
fifth, and ninth lunar months; specifically,
on the first day of each of these months.
Alternatively, one may begin the sketching on the fifteenth day;
the location for the painted image should be within a Buddha hall or in a mountain hermitage.
In this location, mark out an area of one hundred paces square.
It must be free from all foul odors and impurities; the water there must likewise be free of insects, clean, pure, and beautiful.
On the ground where the painting is to be made, sprinkle and smear it daily with fragrant water according to the ritual rules.
The painters shall have their faculties well-proportioned and be of a truly virtuous and upright nature, endowed with the five faculties of faith.
When applying the pigments, they shall observe the eightfold precepts of the fast;
they shall bathe once and put on fresh, clean garments.
Cease all further discussion.
First, in the center, paint a Bodhi tree,
its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits adorned with various jewels.
They were like wish-fulfilling trees interspersed with various differences,
having branches and twigs made of the seven jewels and flowers and leaves made of many precious gems,
with white pearls for their anthers and red pearls for their filaments.
Various jewels and lapis lazuli serve as its fruits;
some branches produce fruits made of diverse jewels,
while other branches produce sprouts made of diverse jewels.
Some branches give rise to clouds of various jewels;
some branches rain down droplets of nectar;
and some branches hang with the celestial garments of the gods.
Some branches hung with precious bells and chimes;
some branches produced coral, amber, red pearls, and agate;
and between every branch, clouds, light, and lightning were painted.
Upon the branches, leaves, and flowers, one should further paint white cranes, peacocks, *kalaviṅkas*, parrots, *śārikas*, *jīvañjīvakas*, and various other beautiful birds.
On the ground, one should paint the seven treasures, adorning it everywhere with colorful ornamentation.
In this manner, beneath a tree on the ground, one should paint Śākyamuni Tathāgata,
complete with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor excellencies,
his body surrounded by a halo, seated upon a lion throne.
Seated in the full lotus posture with the mudrā of preaching the Dharma,
his eyes gaze upon the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Rāja;
from the crown of his head, he emits great flames of multicolored light.
One should bend the upper part of the right hand and raise the palm.
The tips of the thumb and middle finger should be pressed together,
while the remaining three fingers are slightly bent and extended apart.
The left hand is raised upon the left knee,
bestowing fearlessness.
To the right side of the Buddha, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is depicted.
With a serene and joyful countenance, he sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka),
holding a white fly-whisk (śveta-cāmara).
To the left of the Buddha, one should paint the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
With a serene and joyful countenance, he sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) holding a white fly-whisk (śveta-cāmara).
To the right of the Buddha’s seat, one should paint the Ekākṣarocchuṣmavijaya-rāja.
His body is golden in color as he gazes up at the Tathāgata.
In his left hand he holds an opened lotus flower,
upon the center of which a single golden wheel is depicted standing upright.
With his right hand raised in the gesture of the open palm and his body surrounded by a circular halo,
he stands before the Buddha’s seat;
to his left, one should paint the White Parasol Sovereign of the Peak Mandala (Śvetachatra-Uṣṇīṣacakravartin).
Visualize the One-Syllable Cakravartin King with a golden-colored body;
his left hand is held at the chest grasping an opened lotus flower,
upon the calyx of which a white parasol is painted.
His right hand holds a half-open lotus flower that has not yet fully blossomed;
his back is adorned with a circular halo.
Furthermore, following this is the White Parasol Sovereign of the Uṣṇīṣa.
Paint the King of the Uṣṇīṣa Cakra;
his body is golden in appearance,
gazing toward the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakra King.
Her left hand holds a bimba fruit,
and her right hand holds a blue utpala lotus;
she has a circular halo behind her body.
Furthermore, after the One-Syllable Cakravartin King,
paint the Light-Cluster Cakravartin King,
whose body is golden in appearance.
Behold the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.
His left hand holds an opened lotus flower;
upon the calyx of the flower, paint the Buddha’s heart-seal (hṛdaya-mudrā).
Surrounded by flames,
his right hand holds a cintāmaṇi jewel at his chest;
his body is encircled by a halo of various colors.
Furthermore, after the King of the Crown of the Mass of Light,
one should paint the Victorious King of the Crown,
his body golden in color.
The left hand holds an opened lotus flower,
upon the calyx of which a sword is drawn upright;
the right hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
With a halo behind his body,
he gazes upon the One-Syllable Cakravartin King;
these five Cakravartin Kings have faces that are serene and joyful.
Their physical forms and ornamental colors are exactly like those of bodhisattvas;
they are adorned with crowns, necklaces, bracelets, and garments,
and all sit in the half-lotus posture upon white lotuses.
Furthermore, to the right of the One-Syllable Cakravartin,
one should paint the deity Senāpati,
his face serene and joyful, gazing toward the One-Syllable Cakravartin.
In his left hand at the side of his chest he holds a spear,
upon which are painted hanging silk streamers;
in his right hand he holds a vajra.
Clad in armor and seated in the half-lotus posture,
one should also paint the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara to the right side of the Buddha’s seat.
The body is white-yellow in color and sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
With his left hand at his chest, he holds an opened lotus flower;
with his right hand, he raises his palm while bowing his body to gaze upon the Buddha.
Furthermore, to the left of the Buddha’s seat,
one should depict the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi;
his body is purple-red in color, and he sits in the full lotus posture.
With his left hand at his chest holding a vajra,
his right hand raised with the palm facing upward, and his body slightly bent as he gazes toward the Buddha;
he is positioned behind Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Paint the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumāra with his left hand at his chest holding an opened lotus flower;
upon the calyx of the flower, depict a three-pronged vajra standing upright.
Bend the right elbow and turn the palm upward;
join the tips of the thumb and middle finger together,
while the remaining three fingers are slightly bent and extended.
Next, paint the Bodhisattva Vimalamati.
In her left hand she holds an opening lotus;
upon the flower’s pedestal, she draws a conch shell standing upright and inverted.
The right hand is bent with the upper side raised toward the palm.
Next, one should depict the Bodhisattva Śāntimatī,
holding a vajra at her chest with her left hand.
The right hand is raised upward upon the right thigh.
Next, paint the Bodhisattva Amitaprajñā,
whose left hand holds an open lotus flower at the side of his chest.
On the side of the flower pedestal, draw a wheel standing upright;
the right hand holds a cintāmaṇi jewel.
Next, draw the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
The left hand is held at the chest grasping a flower;
the right hand holds a cintāmaṇi jewel raised above the right thigh.
Next, paint the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja-vimala.
The left hand holds a vajra,
and the right hand has its palm raised.
Next, paint the Bodhisattva Mahāmati.
The left hand holds an open lotus flower;
upon the calyx of the flower, draw a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) surrounded by flames.
The palms of their right hands are turned upward.
These bodhisattvas have joyful countenances and golden-colored bodies,
each adorned with jeweled crowns, necklaces, and bracelets.
Adorned with various garments of diverse colors,
he sat upon a precious lotus flower in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka),
positioned behind Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Paint the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā,
her face gentle and compassionate as she gazes upward at the assembly;
her left hand holds an opened lotus flower.
Upon the flower pedestal, draw the Buddha’s heart-seal (hṛdaya-mudrā).
On both sides of the seal, draw an eye each.
The right hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi).
Next, paint the Bodhisattva with the ūrṇā-kośa mark;
his face and eyes are compassionate and gentle,
and his left hand holds an opened lotus flower.
Upon the flower pedestal, draw the seal of the Buddha’s ūrṇā-kośa (hair-treasure) surrounded by flames.
The right hand is held in a hollow fist against the upper part of the right flank.
Visualize the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.
Next, paint the Bodhisattva Ruciraśūla,
whose face is compassionate and gentle;
his left hand is placed at the navel.
In his right hand he holds a lance,
upon which a hanging silk banner is depicted;
next, the Bodhisattva Dantamati is painted.
His face is compassionate and gentle.
His left hand holds an opened lotus flower,
upon the calyx of which is painted the mudrā of the Buddha’s tooth.
With his right hand placed at his chest,
he sits beneath the seat of the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā;
there, one should paint the Great Mantra King Sunārī.
His countenance is compassionate and gentle;
his left hand holds a vajra,
and his right hand grasps a lotus flower as he gazes upon the Tathāgata.
These bodhisattvas possess bodies of golden hue;
each is adorned with flower crowns, necklaces, bracelets,
armlets, and various garments of diverse colors and patterns.
He sits upon a precious lotus flower in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*).
Furthermore, behind the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi,
one should paint the youth Kumārakrodhavajra.
Paint the Vajra-yakṣa youth;
paint the Subāhu-vajra youth; paint the Mārīcī-vajra youth.
These four youths are of a brilliant crimson hue;
each holds a vajra, their countenances are joyful and serene,
and they are all adorned with flower garlands, precious necklaces, bracelets, and armlets.
Adorned with exquisite celestial garments and ornaments,
he sits upon a lotus throne in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka).
Furthermore, behind Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva...
Paint the Great Mantra King of Avalokiteśvara with the Horse Head:
his body is deep purple-red, his face is wrathful,
and his right hand, held upright at his chest, grasps a battle-axe.
The right hand is bent upward, grasping a lotus flower;
its petals, stem, and so forth are adorned with snakes as necklaces.
On the wrists are jeweled bracelets, and on the upper arms are jeweled bands.
Wearing a flower crown upon his head and garments around his waist,
he sits upon a precious lotus flower and gazes toward the One-Syllable Cakravartin King,
positioned behind Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara.
Paint the Bodhisattva Sūnāri holding a lotus;
her body is white-yellow in color, her countenance is compassionate and gentle,
and her right hand grasps a noose.
With the left hand extended downward, he sits upon a lotus throne.
Following the Bodhisattva Sunāri,
one should paint the deity Parṇaśavarī.
Her body is greenish-blue in color, her countenance is compassionate and gentle,
and she has four hands,
one of which holds a noose.
A battle-axe;
a precious fruit;
and the bestowing of fearlessness.
Seated upon a lotus throne,
to the left of the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin,
one should paint the wrathful king Aparājita.
He has four faces and four arms, his body is white in appearance,
and he displays a protruding belly.
His form— with arms, hands, and legs— is short like that of a dwarf elephant.
The waist was painted with tiger skin, and snake-heads served as ear-ornaments.
The Naga King Takṣaka formed his waist-cord,
and the Naga King Vāsuki formed his shoulder-wrap.
Various venomous snakes adorn his body, arms, and calves;
he wears a crown of matted hair, his entire body is ablaze with flames, and he stands upon a red lotus flower.
His first right hand holds a vajra.
The right second hand forms a fist with the middle, ring, and little fingers;
the thumb presses down upon them.
The index finger is extended straight upward as the elbow is bent.
The first left hand holds a three-pronged trident;
the second left hand holds a battle-axe.
The central face is fierce, with wide-open eyes and a gaping mouth.
Emitting manifold rays of light, one gazes upon the Tathāgata;
on the right side, one gazes upon the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin;
and on the left side, one gazes upon the one who recites the mantra.
Above [the central deity], depict the assembly of the Buddha Avalokiteśvara;
below the Wrathful King (Krodharāja),
paint the Earth Deity (Pṛthivīdevatā).
His countenance is serene and joyful, and his body is white in color.
His left hand is held at his chest grasping a precious casket;
his right hand is bent upward with the palm facing forward, holding a precious water-pitcher.
From his mouth issued forth lotus flowers with stalks and leaves;
he knelt upright and sat upon a precious ground,
following after the earth deities.
Paint the deity of the Hiraṇyavatī River with a joyful countenance and a body of pure white color;
he stands with palms joined in reverence, and upon his head are painted seven serpent heads.
Next, after the deity of the Hiraṇyavatī River,
paint the seven-headed Nāga King Kālika and the seven-headed Nāga King Mucilinda.
Kneeling with their right knees on the ground, they gazed up at the Tathāgata.
One held a cluster of precious flowers and the other held a cluster of precious jewels;
these two were the Dragon Kings Guhyapati and Mucilinda.
They have already made offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas,
and furthermore, they have done so under the guidance of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secret Traces.
Paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the King of the Most Victorious Vidya-rājas.
His body is reddish-yellow; his brows are knit and his eyes are wrathful.
There is a single eye between his eyebrows, and his canine fangs protrude upward.
Seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*),
his right hand rests upon a long sword,
and his left hand holds a vajra at his chest.
Next, paint the Bodhisattva Bhīṣaṇavajra.
His body is reddish-yellow; his brows are knit and his eyes are wrathful.
His canine fangs protrude upward, and he sits in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*).
His right hand holds a three-pronged trident;
his left hand is raised and bent, grasping a single-pronged vajra.
Next, paint the Bodhisattva Yellow-Eyed Vajra.
The body is white-yellow in color and the facial expression is serene and joyful;
he sits in the half-lotus posture with his right arm bent at the elbow, the palm raised toward the inside.
The left hand is extended and bent, resting upon the upper part of the left flank,

their physical karma will become pure, and they will achieve the ocean of wisdom and merit of the King-Crown Samādhi.
Surpassing all that is most excellent and extraordinary,
they shall be honored, revered, and praised immeasurably by devas and humans;
they shall realize the stage of Buddhahood and never again regress.
When one who has realized this mantra glares with eyes wide in wrath and utters a thunderous roar,
all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of spirits and deities become terrified and flee in all directions.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, sees that person approaching, he...
They share their seats and sit together with them;
all those great devas likewise share their seats.
When the devas of the three realms see this person approaching, they [welcome them].
If those who are arrogant and rebellious do not rise to welcome and pay respect,
their heads shall all shatter like the branches of the *lāṅgalī* flower.
Even if I were to remain for billions of *koṭi* great eons...
Even praising this mantra cannot fully exhaust its qualities.
One who accomplishes this mantra is said to have realized the supreme siddhi.
They shall dwell in the *trāyastriṃśa-deva* lifespan and the *mahānārāyaṇa-samādhi*.
His life shall remain secure and eternal, free from the calamity of death;
having completed his tenure as a celestial sovereign, he will transform his body like a Buddha,
realize the five supernormal powers, and depart from this heavenly realm.
Surrounded before and behind by immeasurable [attendants],
they travel to various Buddha-fields,
manifesting diverse transformations to guide and attract sentient beings.
In accordance with the various Buddha-fields,
he manifests the body of Śakra,
or the body of Vajrapāṇi, or the body of Mahābrahmā.
Sometimes they manifest in the body of the god Īśvara;
sometimes they manifest in the bodies of boys or girls;
and sometimes they enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Manifesting various bodies as appropriate, they rescue and liberate all sentient beings;
in mountain forests, cities, towns, and villages, they provide dwellings and supply them with various kinds of food and clothing for their relief and sustenance.
Constantly acting as a refuge for the three realms,
delivering all sentient beings,
and possessing the five supernormal powers, they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Chapter Seven: The Accomplishment of Seals (Mudrā-siddhi).
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni...
He addressed the great assembly:
"O sons of noble family, you should receive and uphold the immeasurable and innumerable power of great valor of the Samādhi of the Manifestation of All Tathāgatas."
All Tathāgatas abide in the body of mantras.
This is the true lineage of all Tathāgatas, an immeasurable and boundless, unprecedented dharma.
It is the Great Seal and Sealing Mantra that gives rise to and disseminates infinite majestic power.
Within this, there is the samādhi-door of the Great Dharma-Crown that can give rise to all the supernatural powers and all the stages of realization of all bodhisattvas,
and can destroy all koṭis of māra-armies.
It is that which can encompass all the great bodhisattvas who possess the power of great heroes;
it is that which assists and protects them;
and it is that which can cause all terrifying sentient beings to give rise to a mind of great compassion.
"Sons of good family, I shall now briefly explain the Great Seal and Seal-Mantra that accomplishes all activities and possesses great majestic power.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secret Traces, [spoke].
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that you will explain the Great Seal and Seal-Mantra of the Pervasive Majestic Virtue of all Tathāgatas,
so that all sentient beings may, through minimal effort, achieve great realization for their benefit."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of the Secret Trace, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and maintain it with meditative concentration.
I shall now, for your sake, analyze and explain the dhāraṇī-seal methods of the Great Vigor of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
The First of the Heart Vajra-Exertion Mudrās of All Tathāgatas:
With the left and right hands, interlace the eight fingers such that the right presses over the left and they enter into the palms.
Quickly clench the fists;
with the two thumbs placed side by side,
extend them flat and press them against the middle joints of the sides of the right index fingers.
Do not allow the head to bend.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namo sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ (1) | Imira (2) | Huṃ hūṃ (3) | Yaṃ kham (4). As for this mudrā, join the tips of the two thumbs.
Moving up and down together, this is called the Seal-Mantra for Invoking the Tathāgata Lineage. It is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ īdṛśe*. These two constitute the seal and the mantra.
This is called the Tathāgata’s mind of supreme diligence;
its power is able to deliver all beings from the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals,
and it can also assist in accomplishing the meritorious deeds and activities of all Tathāgatas.

It encompasses all bodhisattvas, including Śakra, Brahmā, Īśvara, the King of the Yama Heaven, the Kings of the Fire, Water, Wind, and Vaiśravaṇa Heavens, up to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the tenth stage, Maheśvara, and others.
The second mudrā of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: Following the previous heart-mudrā,
simply change the left thumb by bending it into the palm.
Grasp the tip of the right index finger.
With the right thumb positioned as before in the seal of concentration, recite the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ jvala*. If this seal is modified by changing the position of the right thumb, [the mantra remains the same].
Moving up, down, coming,
and going is called the Family Seal for Invoking Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Regarding the three Vajra Guhyapatis Bodhisattvas’ seals, they follow the previous heart-seals as prescribed.
One should change the left thumb as before,
extending and pressing it;
the right thumb is then bent and inserted into the palm.
Grasp the left index finger;
the left thumb remains extended as previously fixed.
The mudrā-mantra is as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ vajra-jvālāmukhi. If one changes the position of the left thumb-tip, it constitutes the mudrā.
Moving up, down, coming, and going is called the Seal of the Family of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of the Secret Traces;
this is the fourth of the Seals of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin. Furthermore, one should join the palms.
With the two ring fingers and the two little fingers,
cross the right over the left and insert them into the palms;
then, extend the two middle fingers straight upward.
Bend each first joint so that the tips touch one another;
then place the two thumbs side by side within the palms.
Extend them flat.
Then, bend the two index fingers flat and press them against the backs of the two thumbs.
The mudrā for joining the index fingers together is as follows; the mantra is:
Namaḥ prajñe dharādhiṣṭhite ṛddhivikurvaṇāya oṃ hūṃ tāḥ.

24. *puṇḍarīkani*. 25. *kumārīṇi* (the *ṇi* follows as above). 26. *āpadākitasatsenatara*. 27. *dhā*.
*Li ni* (27) *huṃ* (28). This is the Great Root Seal-Mantra of the King of the Uṣṇīṣa Wheel.
It was previously spoken and upheld by all Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā River.
All Tathāgatas of the future shall together proclaim and uphold it;
all Tathāgatas of the present now together proclaim and uphold it,
for the purpose of gathering and guiding all sentient beings.
It is taught that this is equally maintained by the wise as their dwelling place;
when one forms this seal, all jealous, evil, obstructing vināyakas shall not draw near.
Guhya-pati, this is the Great Root Seal of the King of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakra.
All Buddhas, remaining for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Gaṅgā-sand numbers of kalpas,
have praised and expounded the merit and spiritual power of this seal.
Nor can it be exhausted.
Furthermore, even by employing various words and metaphors,
one cannot fully describe this Great Seal (Mahāmudrā).
If a wise person holds this seal and recites the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King,
they will never be troubled or disturbed by hundreds of thousands of millions of māras or their hosts.
After a hundred thousand koṭis of great kalpas, this person shall not fall into the evil realms. Why is this?
Because of the mass of merit and virtue obtained by this person.
I could not exhaustively describe this Great One-Syllable Cakravartin King Mantra even were I to speak for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of great kalpas.
If there should be anyone who, with a single pure mind, [recites it]...
For one who maintains the precepts with diligence and constantly recites and upholds [this teaching],
the power of mindfulness, the power of wisdom,
and the power of insight that they obtain will persist through all places of birth for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas.
It is never lost or regressed.
Why? Because this Great Seal possesses great majestic power, great efficacy, and immeasurable strength.
The fifth mudrā of the High-Crested Wheel-Turning King: furthermore, with the two ring fingers and the two little fingers of both hands, cross the right over the left and insert them into the palms.
Next, straighten the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another.
Place the two thumbs side by side and extend them to press down upon the sides of the middle joints of the two ring fingers.
Furthermore, place both index fingers on the middle joints of the sides of the middle fingers and bend the tips so they touch;
the mudrā and mantra are as follows:

Namo samantabuddhānām | Oṃ hūṃ jvala-jvala-tuṇḍe miṅ-mi-ra-ghoṣa-svare duna-duna hūṃ || [This is the seal of the White Parasol Cūḍāmaṇi-rāja; it is performed according to the previous High-Crested King seal.]
One should adjust the two middle fingers so that their first joints are slightly bent and their tips meet flatly against one another.
Next, extend the two index fingers, leaving them half an inch apart. The mantra for this seal is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ mama mama hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the Seal of the Seven-Rayed Uṣṇīṣa King; it is also called the Seal of the Golden Wheel Uṣṇīṣa, which is performed according to the previous High Uṣṇīṣa King Seal.
Only change the two index fingers:
spread them apart, hold them upright,
and extend their tips so that each is separated from the tip of the middle finger.
The mudrā for the one and two-tenths inches [in size] is as follows: The mantra is:
Oṃ. This is the eighth mudrā of the Victorious Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin;
it is performed according to the previous method of the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin mudrā.
Simply modify the two index fingers by bending them flat against the first joint of the middle fingers,
their tips touching; the mudrā and mantra are as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ hūṃ jhaḥ svariṣa jvala jvala bandha bandha namaḥ namaḥ dhuru hūṃ dhuru hūṃ dhuru hūṃ ho ha na huṃ.* Regarding the ninefold turning of the Dharma-wheel mudrā: one should also employ the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin, using the two little fingers of both hands.
The palms are placed flat together with the heads of the hands touching.
Next, the two ring fingers are each bent and inserted into the palms.
The two middle fingers are each slightly bent and held upright.
The tips [of the fingers] touch one another.
The two index fingers are placed against the side above the middle joint of the middle fingers,
their tips touching.
Place each of the two thumbs upon the two ring fingers;
open the palms so that the wrists are four inches apart.
This is a dharma-mudrā capable of turning the wheel of the twelve aspects of existence.
He extinguishes all defilements and obstructions, becoming equal to the Tathāgata.
[This is] the tenth application of the Vajra-pestle that crushes afflictions seal. For the one-syllable Cakravartin mantra, perform it according to the Cakravartin seal.
Next, straighten and join the tips of the two middle fingers.
Then, place the two index fingers behind the backs of the two middle fingers.
The heads are pressed together;
this is one *dharmamudrā*, also called the *āsana-mudrā*.
Lord Guhyapati, these are the five great *mudrās*.
It is called the Great Seal of the King of the Family of Mantras of the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakra-Rāja of All Tathāgatas;
alternatively, it is called the Seal of the High Uṣṇīṣa-Cakra-Rāja,
and the Seal of the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa-Cakra-Rāja.
The third is named the Seal of the King of the Summit of the Mass of Light;
the fourth is named the Seal of Turning the Wheel of Dharma;
the fifth is named the Seal that Shatters Afflictions like Hailstones.
These mudrās and so forth are called the Great Cakravartin Mudrā.
Regarding the eleven Great Heart Mudrās of the Tathāgata, the eleventh is according to the first Tathāgata Heart Mudrā mentioned previously.
Only change the two thumbs,
bending them double and inserting them into the palms;
this is the single dharma-seal named the Tathāgata-heart Great Vigor Seal.
If the mantra-practitioner constantly forms this mudrā while reciting the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin mantra,
they should perform one recitation and one mudrā upon their heart center.
If one recites this one hundred and eight times,
one will be able to destroy all fundamental grave offenses of the past and present.
One should always employ this seal for all dharmas.
It protects the body.
The mantra and seal are as follows:
Namo samanta-buddhānām | Oṃ hūṃ guṇale mire svāhā. This is the dharma-mantra.
Its efficacy is the same as that of the first seal and mantra mentioned previously;
it may also be used interchangeably at the site of ritual practice,
for this mantra possesses great majestic power.
Twelfth, the Heart Mudrā of Sarvavid Vairocana: Again, join the palms at the heart;
within the great hollow of the palms.
Furthermore, with the eight fingers of both hands,
bend each flatly so that the tips touch one another;
the distance between these eight fingers should be three *aṅgulas*.
With the two thumbs likewise separated by three *aṅgula*, extend them straight upward; the mantra for this seal is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ jvala hūṃ bandha svāhā*. This dharma-seal and mantra can also accomplish all activities.
Protecting oneself and protecting others, because one binds and cultivates all dharmas to remain free from obstacles and afflictions.
This is the thirteenth seal of the Tathāgata’s mendicant’s staff (khakkhara). Furthermore, with the right thumb...
Bend the fingers across and insert them into the palm;
then, with the index, middle, ring, and little fingers,
grasp tightly to form a fist.
Bend the elbow forward.
Extend the left hand flat to grasp the corner of the *kāṣāya*,
with the head protruding four inches.
Bend the elbows forward and extend the hands flatly; the mantra for this seal is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ dhanu-ṅkārāṇa huṃ phaṭ*. This is the mantra of the Dharma-seal. If one encounters any malevolent sentient beings, [one should recite it].
Then, having bound this mudrā, one uses it to protect the body.
Regarding the fourteenth Tathāgata Alms-bowl Mudrā: first, place the right hand at the heart with the palm facing upward.
Next, cover the right palm with the left hand;
let the tip of the left little finger touch the tip of the right thumb.
Place the tip of the left thumb against the tip of the right little finger.
The mudrā mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ hūṃ rucanapraladhiṣṭhe dhara dhara mahānubhāva buddhapratira svāhā. This dharma-seal mantra possesses great vigor.
One shall always be protected by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas.
Form this mudrā with the wheel and recite this mantra;
at the conclusion of each repetition, call to mind those in the hells and the hungry ghosts.
If sentient beings recite this one hundred and eight times,
then all those in the hells and hungry ghosts shall obtain food and be fully satiated. Furthermore,
if one travels through a wilderness while binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra, [the same result shall be achieved].
Then one will attain the state where all ghosts and spirits in the wilderness do not cause disturbance or affliction.
This is the fifteenth seal of the Tathāgata’s marks and signs. Furthermore, using the two middle fingers, the two ring fingers, and the two little fingers of both hands...
Press the right hand over the left, interlace the fingers,
and insert them into the palms.
Clasp each palm together and extend both index fingers straight upward.
The sides of the heads are pressed together.
Each of these two thumbs presses against the side of the index finger.
With the seal inverted and the palms facing upward, place it upon the forehead.
Place the tips of the two index fingers directly at the space between the eyebrows. The mantra is as follows:

Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyas-tathāgatānāṃ samyaksaṃbuddhānāṃ hī-hī hī-hī panta-panta tiṣṭha tiṣṭha dhara-dhara nirdhana-dhana-maṇi svāhā. This dharma-mantra seal is named "The Physical Marks and Signs of a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa-vyañjana). (Note: Regarding the pronunciation of specific characters: *hī* is to be pronounced with an angry tone; *nirdhana* is to be pronounced by curling the tongue; *dhara* is to be pronounced with the initial *d* aspirated.)
If one is constantly able to turn and bind this seal,
one will swiftly accomplish all *siddhis* and possess great majestic power.
If one seals the crown of the head with this mudrā,
it is called the Tathāgata-ushṇīṣa-mudrā;
if one seals the nose with it, [it is called the Tathāgata-nāsā-mudrā].
The mantra for the Tathāgata’s Nose-Seal on the Crown is as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ hūṃ īriṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the Tathāgata’s Nose-Seal on the Crown.
By constantly binding this protection upon the body,
one shall, throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of great kalpas and in whatever place one is born,
never suffer from ailments such as diseases of the head or nose.
The Sixteenth Tathāgata-Eye Mudrā Mantra: Furthermore, join the two hands in *añjali*;
bend both thumbs double and insert them into the palms.
Next, bend the first joints of both index fingers;
press their tips against the middle phalanges on the sides of the middle fingers,
with the tips of the two index fingers separated by one inch.
This is the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Eye.
When bound upon the pure wheel of the Cakravartin Maṇḍala,
it is able to bring great benefit and extinguish all grave sins.
To accomplish the siddhi of the mantra of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin:

whatever merit has been cultivated over hundreds of thousands of koṭis of past kalpas shall all be drawn in and gathered together through the power of the mudrā. The mudrā-mantra is as follows: [Mantra]

*Namo sarvatathāgatādhipate vajrapāṇaye samyaksaṃbuddhāya. Oṃ hūṃ ruru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārthasādhani svāhā.* O Lord of Guhyakas, this is the Great Vidyārājñī-mantra of the Eye of the Tathāgata.
These ten koṭis of Buddhas have all together proclaimed it.
In the past, when I was a bodhisattva,
at the abodes of ten koṭis of Buddhas...
Having received this mantra,
if one who recites it should always maintain a mind of great diligence, [they shall attain success].
By reciting and upholding this mantra,
all the mantra-deities of the bodhisattvas will appear before one, and all the mantra-classes of the Vajra family will likewise be accomplished.
Therefore, those who uphold the mantra of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin, Guhyapāda,
should first recite this mantra seven times, or two, three, or seven times each [session].
This is the Great Vidyārājñī-mantra of the Tathāgata’s Eye.
The Tathāgata now speaks this for the sake of all sentient beings attaining great peace and happiness, and for becoming free from defilement and pure.
If a practitioner encounters a person of violent and evil nature,
they should touch their face with their hand while silently reciting this mantra.
One will attain joy through the common logic [of this teaching] and will also be able to subdue all malevolent spirits, such as *chimei* and *wangliang*. Guhyapati,

if there is a person who recites and maintains the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King, yet fails to achieve the realization of their first or second requested dharma, [the following shall be done].
Then one should add this mantra of the Great Vidyārāja and recite it together with [the other] equally for two hundred thousand times;
one will certainly achieve the supreme siddhi of the mantra of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin.
If one recites both [mantras] together without first performing these one or two ritual procedures,
then misfortune will follow and harm the body of the mantra-reciter.
The Seventeenth: The Tathāgata Ūrṇā-kośa Seal Mantra. This is identical to the Tathāgata Netra Seal, with the exception that the two index fingers are modified.
Place each [finger] upon the back of the middle finger, with the tips separated from the middle finger joints by one *aṅgula*. The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ hrīḥ huṃ*. This is the mantra of the ūrṇā (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows) of the Tathāgata.
This has indeed been proclaimed by all the Tathāgatas of the past;
I now proclaim it as well.
When turning this seal:
Even the Great Lord Maheśvara, Kumāra, and Śikhin do not cause him affliction;
how much less so the various minor demons, goblins, and spirits?
And what would cause distress?
