The eighteen mudrās of the Tathāgata’s mouth are modeled upon the eighteen mudrās of the Tathāgata’s heart,
with the sole modification being the two thumbs.
With both shoulders squared and arms extended,
bend the joints of the head [of the fingers] equally so that they are positioned alongside the side of the right index finger.
Place the two thumbs at the space between three grains of barley at the mouth-opening;
this refers to the joint at the tip of the back of the two thumbs.
The mantra for the Seal of the Lips is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānāṃ kili kili huṃ hūṃ svāhā. This seal and mantra possess a great flaming torch.
It can swiftly assist in accomplishing all undertakings.
If the mantra-practitioner constantly forms this seal and recites while holding it before his mouth, [the goal will be achieved].
Recite this oral mantra twenty-one times.
Thereafter, when reciting the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King,
by the power of the mudrā and the mantra—
All humans and devas within the three realms who see, hear,
or engage in discourse with them will all feel respect and affection; therefore, such a person should always speak with harmony, elegance, truthfulness, gentleness, and the Dharma.
For a thousand million *koṭi* aeons, such a person shall suffer no affliction of the mouth.
When Mahādeva, Viṣṇu, and all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of spirits hear the speech of this person, [they shall be moved].
Even they shall all be reverently subdued;
how much more so other minor goblins, demons, and spirits.
Regarding the nineteenth seal of the King of Unconquerable Wrath: one should place the right knee upon the ground.
The left foot treads upon the ground;
he assumes the posture of being about to rise and lean forward, with his face turned upward and eyes glaring in anger,
looking askance toward the left side.
One should use the right arm,
with the fingers pointing to the right and toward the back,
extending the forearm obliquely.
In a state of urgent wrath,
he raises his arm as if to strike the ground;
his five fingers are spread wide and extended in a furious grip.
The palms are positioned as if covering or tilted sideways.
Next, with the left arm, turn the left side toward the back and raise the arm with great force.
Bend the arm upward;
the five fingers are slightly spread apart.
Extend the fingers upward and spread them apart,
with the palms facing forward.
When forming this mudrā:
If one utters a great roar of anger,
reciting the two syllables "Huṃ" twenty-one times,
all obstructing karmic offenses will be utterly destroyed.
The Māra kings of the desire realm and their military commanders have all been utterly crushed.
In the past, when I first went to the Nairañjanā River,
I bathed my body and proceeded to this foot of the Bodhi tree.
While seated upon the Vajrāsana,
at that time there shall be immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Māra kings and their demonic hosts,
each assuming various foul, impure, and wrathful appearances.
When she was tormenting and terrifying me,
the Invincible Wrathful King (Durjayakrodharāja) suddenly surged forth from the earth before me,
assuming the form of a celestial maiden.
Sealing this with the seal of the fetter of hatred,
one crushes all hosts of māras;
their various terrifying forms are simultaneously dispersed and extinguished.
There was no one able to cause me distress.
During that night, from midnight until the break of dawn,
I fully realized unsurpassed, perfect wisdom.
Observing that among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world there is no one who has attained realization,
the mantra for the Seal that Subdues Māra is as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ hūṃ | Tura tura | Caṇḍanirmaryāde hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | This is the mantra of the Wrathful King Durjaya, the Lord of Guhyakas.
This is what I have taught.
If a practitioner of mantras should encounter a place of great terror inhabited by evil spirits and ghosts,
and desires to protect their own body, establish a boundary, and provide guardianship for those performing the ritual practice:
One should diligently apply oneself with vigor to maintain this seal and recite this mantra.
By proceeding to cultivate this dharma,
one will be free from obstacles and afflictions, and quickly attain accomplishment.
The twenty mudrās of the Tathāgata Spear: For the twenty mudrās of the Tathāgata Spear, the body is upright and seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
With the left hand, the palm is turned upward and held horizontally beneath the navel.
The four fingers are joined together and extended straight;
the thumb is slightly bent and extended straight,
pressed against the side of the base of the index finger.
Next, with the right hand, join the tips of the thumb and index finger;
keep the middle, ring, and little fingers together,
extending them slightly as if they were bent.
The tips of the thumb and index finger of the right hand and the little finger of the left hand are pressed together;
this is a single dharmamudrā.
If a wise person constantly maintains these bonds, they will never again lose their power of faith, diligence, and wisdom, nor the power of the Tathāgata’s practice throughout future births.
They shall receive the protective mindfulness of all Tathāgatas, who bestow this seal-mantra: [Mantra follows]
*Namo samanta-buddhānām. Oṃ hūṃ viraje mahāśodhani tura dhara huṃ phaṭ. Virajini phaṭ. Maṅgale phaṭ. Svāhā.* This dharma-mantra should be recited three times each day for twenty-one days.
Because one swiftly attains the supreme accomplishment free from obstacles within the three realms.
The twenty-first, the Tathāgata Navel Seal, is identical to the Tathāgata Spear Seal.
Only change the tips of the right hand’s thumb and index finger so that they are separated from the tip of the left hand’s little finger by the distance of a single grain of barley.
This Dharma-seal is also called the Great Supernatural Power Seal of all Buddhas.
If a wise person constantly recollects and maintains it,
they should form this seal and recite this mantra.
Then one shall obtain the elimination of malarial fevers lasting one or two days, the disease of jaundice, ailments of the abdomen and head, and all such diseases.
Furthermore, all calamities and obstacles shall naturally be extinguished.
The seal-mantra for receiving blessings, long life, peace, and abundant joy is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ hūṃ jñe jñe svāhā*. This is the dharma-mantra.
One can manifest the inconceivable supernatural transformations of the Tathāgata’s various forms and types to comfort sentient beings.
Regarding the twenty-second seal of the Tathāgata’s Armor: one should place the right hand at the heart.
Place the thumb across and bent within the palm.
With the index, middle, ring, and little fingers,
firmly grasp the thumb to form a fist.
This single Dharma-seal is named the Supreme Universal Cakravartin Heart Seal.
If a wise person constantly seals the crown of the head, the nape of the neck, the left and right shoulders,
and the heart center with this seal, [the benefits shall be obtained].
This causes the holder to attain great power.
Although a practitioner may diligently cultivate the dharma according to the ritual rules,
if they lack this seal, they will lack adornment.
It is like a body that is naked and ugly; like a country without a king;
like a house with no one inside; like food without salt;
like a pond that has dried up; like the earth being empty and devoid of groves, flowers, and grasses.
Just as a fire-worshipping Brahmin heretic has no dharma upon which to rely,
and just as a king riding in a chariot has no driver to control it,
so it is with the wise person who, despite being diligent, [lacks such guidance].
If one lacks the seal of the armor (*kavaca-mudrā*), one will be afflicted by Māra and achieve no efficacy. The mantra for this seal is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, oṃ hūṃ trayaṃ praveśa jvala huṃ hūṃ*. This dharma-mantra is named the Tathāgata-vajrapada-samādhi.
It is constantly used for self-protection;
just as a king clad in armor and equipped with formidable weapons has no fear of evil bandits or enemy troops.
In this same way, the wise one should likewise do so:
three times each day, they should measure their own strength and the power of the dharma,
and diligently practice this *kavaca-mudrā-mantra* according to the dharma.
This is because one will swiftly achieve accomplishment and be free from fear.
Regarding the twenty-third mudrā, the Tathāgata-Śikhā (Tathāgata Topknot): it follows the previous nail-mudrā, with the sole modification being that the middle finger is extended.
Hold it upright.
Place the seal upon the crown of the head, causing it to stand straight and erect. The mantra for the seal is as follows:
Namo samanta-buddhānām jvala-jvala-tantra-svara-hūṃ. This seal-mantra is named the Power of the Tathāgata-Usnīṣa-Samādhi-Dvāra.
It is capable of accomplishing all ritual activities.
Regarding the twenty-fourth, the Tathāgata Ear Seal: it follows the previous Nail Seal, with the only modification being that the index finger is extended.
Straighten [the fingers] and place the seal upright at the openings of the ears,
level with the upper helixes.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namo sarvatathāgatānāṃ hūḥ. This mudrā and mantra are named the Tathāgata-ear Samādhi-gate.
If one constantly performs this wheel-binding mudrā,
all ear diseases will be swiftly eliminated,
and one shall realize the supernormal power of the divine ear (divya-śrotra-abhijñā).
Regarding the twenty-fifth, the Tathāgata-tooth mudrā: one should use the index, middle, ring, and little fingers of the left hand.
Quickly bend [the fingers] and clench the fist so that no fingernails are exposed.
Furthermore, extend the thumb straight out.
Pressing the head [of the thumb] directly upward,
the first joint on the surface of the thumb's face should be level with the outer back of the index finger.
Place the mudrā on the left jaw;
do the same for the right. The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ tathāgatā daṃṣṭre huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This mudrā and mantra are called the Tathāgata-daṃṣṭra-samādhi-mukha.
Possessing great majestic power,
by reciting this mantra and sealing one's teeth with the *cakra-mudrā*,
one shall obtain the Buddha’s teeth in a future age.
The twenty-sixth, the Tathāgata Head Seal: Furthermore, with the right hand, place the thumb across the tips of the middle, ring, and little fingers.
Extending the index finger straight upward to touch the crown of the head, the mudrā and mantra are as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ murdhni svāhā*. This mudrā and mantra are named the Tathāgata-mūrdha-samādhi-dvāra (The Gate of the Tathāgata’s Crown Samādhi).
The twenty-seventh, the Tathāgata Lip Seal: Furthermore, with the right hand, extend the thumb upright and press it against the side of the index finger.
With the index finger held straight upright,
extend the middle finger so that it appears slightly curved,
and direct the ring finger toward the palm.
Bend [the fingers] into the shape of a hook.
The little finger is bent into the shape of a crescent moon. The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām ā ā va va haṃ*. This mudrā and mantra are named the Tathāgata-oṣṭha-samādhi-mukha (The Gate of the Tathāgata’s Lip Samādhi).
The holder shall thereby attain the eradication of all sins.
Regarding the twenty-eighth Tathāgata-tongue mudrā: furthermore, with the right hand, [one joins] the index, middle, ring, and little fingers.
Place them together so they touch at the heart level;
extend the palms upward and flatten them,
with the thumbs bent across within the palms.
The mudrā consists of pointing the tips of the four fingers outward, and the mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ nara nivartaya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This mudrā and mantra are called the Tathāgata-jihvā-samādhi-mukha (The Gate of the Tathāgata’s Tongue Samādhi).
The holder shall obtain the merit of the Tathāgata’s mark of the tongue being fully perfected.
This is the twenty-ninth mudrā of the Tathāgata’s ribs. Furthermore, one should assist with the right hand by bending the elbow.
With the ring finger and little finger,
double-bend the tips so they rest against the surface of the thumb;
the index and middle fingers are placed side by side, held straight up and extended.
Facing forward with the interlaced-rib mudrā, the mantra is recited as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ haḥ khaṃ*. This mudrā and mantra are called the "Tathāgata-assisted Samādhi Gate."
The Thirty Tathāgata Shoulder Seals: These thirty Tathāgata shoulder seals follow the previous fingernail seals, with the only modification being the arms.
Extending them straight upward, the seal-mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānāṃ vañjihī phaṭ svāhā. This seal-mantra is named the Tathāgata-skandha-samādhi-dvāra.
Because it possesses great supernatural power, is exceptionally courageous, and accomplishes all dharmas.
The thirty-first, the Tathāgata-Āryā Seal: as before, it is based on the fingernail seal (nakhamudrā).
Simply bend the arm and place the fist against the face;
with the seal positioned at the heart, the mantra for the seal is as follows:
Namo samanta-buddhānām vākire. This seal-mantra is named the Tathāgata-stana-samādhi-dvāra.
The Thirty-second Seal of the Tathāgata’s Lower Abdomen: Furthermore, with the right hand, extend it horizontally one cun below the navel with the palm facing upward.
Place the five fingers together;
next, extend the five fingers of the left hand together and press its back against the palm of the right hand.
Place the two hands upon the abdomen and recite the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ nuḥ nuḥ se puḥ se puḥ miṇḍara-paṇi pa-ra-ma-na-ṇi cchanda-ṇi binda-ṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This seal and mantra is called the Tathāgata’s Abdomen Samādhi Gate.
The Thirty-third Tathāgata Backbone Seal: Furthermore, with the thumb of the right hand, press down upon the tips of the index, ring, and little fingers.
Do not allow the nails to be exposed.
Next, place the middle finger horizontally across the top of the thumb.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām | Īkāraṇa kāraṇa-gandha-citrānanda-maṇidhuni svāhā. This mudrā and mantra are named the Tathāgata-pṛṣṭha-samādhi-dvāra (the Gate of the Tathāgata’s Backbone Samādhi).
The Thirty-Fourth Tathāgata Thigh Seal: Following the previous spine seal,
change the placement to press against the nail of the middle finger,
and extend the head of the index finger.
Pressing the thumb against the fingernail, the mantra is recited as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ dhuṭe svāhā*. This seal and mantra are named the Tathāgata-Ūru-Samādhi-dvāra (The Gate of the Tathāgata’s Thigh Samādhi).
The Thirty-Fifth Seal of the Tathāgata’s Knees: Furthermore, with the two hands joined in *añjali*,
place the little fingers together,
with the right pressing down on the left, and bend them into the palms.
The seal-mantra is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ nava-ṅgi padmapāśāya svāhā*. This seal-mantra is named the Tathāgata’s Knee Samādhi Gate.
The thirty-six mudrās of the Tathāgata’s ankles: furthermore, with the two hands joined in *añjali*, [place] each ring finger...
Place the right hand over the left and bend it into the palm.
The mantra for this seal is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ | ṛte ṛte | dṛte | vajra-mukhi-svāhā*. This seal and mantra are called the Tathāgata’s Ankle Samādhi Gate.
The Thirty-Seven Tathāgata Footprints: Furthermore, with both hands joined in *añjali*,
bend each middle finger so that the right presses down upon the left, tucking them into the palms.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namo sarvatathāgatānāṃ oṃ hūṃ vajra-saṃkula-bhuśiṭi nara jvala huṃ svāhā. This mudrā and mantra are named the Tathāgata-pāda-samādhi-mukha (the Gate of the Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Foot).
The Thirty-eighth Seal of the Tathāgata Banner: Furthermore, with the right hand, place the thumb across the tips of the middle, ring, and little fingers.
Extend the index finger straight upward, holding it taut and pointing vertically as one raises the arm.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ khaṅgi*. This mudrā and mantra are called the Tathāgata-Dhvaja-Mudrā Samādhi Gate.
The Thirty-ninth Seal of the Tathāgata’s Reclining Bed: Following the previous Banner Seal, one only alters the index finger.
Pointing it downward toward the chest, the mantra for the seal is as follows:
*Namo samanta-buddhānām. Hrīḥ.* This seal-mantra is named the Tathāgata’s Bedding Samādhi Gate.
The forty Tathāgata-vehicle mudrās: following the previous banner mudrā,
change the arm so that it is bent and placed before the heart.
The mudrā and mantra for extending the arm horizontally are as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ hūṃ ghaṭaṃ ghaṭaṃ oṃ hūṃ*. This mudrā and mantra are named the Tathāgata-yāna-samādhi-mukha.
The forty-first seal of the Tathāgata’s prophecy: again, with the right arm,
bend the elbow against the side of the chest and extend the forearm straight out.
Tightly clench the fist with the index, middle, ring, and little fingers;
extend the thumb upward and bend it slightly.
At a distance of two finger-widths from the side of the head-finger,
this is the Dharma-mudrā of all Tathāgatas of the past and all Tathāgatas of the future.
All Tathāgatas of the present bestow predictions of enlightenment by means of this seal; therefore,
the wise should form this seal.
The seal-mantra for bestowing the prediction of enlightenment upon all sentient beings is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ hūṃ huṃ traṃ phaṭ*. This seal-mantra is capable of accomplishing all the activities of the Tathāgatas.
By the power of this seal-mantra,
in every birth one shall constantly obtain the power of mindfulness, the power of diligence, and the powers of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom,
and the preeminent aggregate of merit; thus, one shall not be vexed or afflicted by any *chimei*, ghosts, or spirits.
The Tathāgata beholds the seal of the nature of all phenomena; this is the forty-second [seal].
Furthermore, with his right hand, he bends the elbow upward.
Bend the tips of the middle fingers so that they touch the tips of the thumbs;
as for the index, ring, and little fingers:
With the hands held side-by-side, pointing straight upward and fully extended, the mantra is recited as follows:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ parasiṃdaka tvaḥ*. This seal and mantra are named the Tathāgata-darśana-sarvadharmatā-samādhi-mukha (The Samādhi Door of the Tathāgata’s Vision of the Nature of All Dharmas).
The forty-third mudrā, the Tathāgata-flame-mark: as in the previous *dṛṣṭimudrā* (seeing-mudrā), with the sole modification that the index finger, ring finger, and little finger are changed.
Spread the palms toward each other and slightly bend them like the crescent of the new moon;
the mudrā and mantra are as follows: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ jvalani svāhā*. This mudrā and mantra is named the Tathāgata-jvālā-samādhi-mukha.
To manifest all phenomena, the Tathāgata’s light-illumination seal is applied forty-four times; furthermore, with the thumb of his right hand...
With the index finger extended upward and pressed against the side of the head,
keep the index finger straight and erect while extending the middle and little fingers.
Extend each hand with the palm facing upward;
bend the fingers like a crescent moon,
with the ring fingers pointing toward the palms.
The mudrā is bent in the shape of a hook, and the mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ maṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This seal and mantra are called "The Tathāgata’s Radiance Illuminating All Samādhi Gates."
Because it manifests as perfection.
Regarding the forty-five mudrās of the Tathāgata-samādhi: furthermore, with the five fingers of the left hand placed together, [one forms the seal].
Place it below the navel,
two barley grains' distance from the ground,
with the palms turned upward, sideways, and fully extended.
Next, with the four fingers of the right hand joined together,
also held sideways and extended flat with the palm facing upward,
press the back of the right hand against the palm of the left hand.
With the right thumb bent across within the palm, the mantra for the seal is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ jotiśaye mīkṣarame svāhā*. This seal and mantra are named the Tathāgata-nābhi-samādhi-mukha (The Gate of the Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Navel).
The Forty-sixth Seal of the Tathāgata’s Vajra Radiant Flame is the same as the preceding Samādhi Seal; however, one modifies it by placing it upon the heart.
The mantra for this seal is: [Mantra].
Namo samantabuddhānāṃ hūṃ jvala vajra pāṇi riṣi ṛṣi. This is the mantra of the Vajrajvālā Seal for the Lord of Secrets.
It is also called the King of Great Mantra-Spells of the Samādhi of the Vajra-Flame Heart of all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present.
All the great Bodhisattvas who have realized the stages, and so forth...
Even the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of spirits, and those of great majestic power are all unable to transgress it,
let alone other inferior malevolent spirits and ghosts.
The Forty-Seventh Seal of the Tathāgata’s Great Compassion: Following the previous spine-seal, change the placement to press against the nail of the middle finger.
Extend the tip of the ring finger and press it upon the nail of the thumb.
For the sake of all sentient beings burdened by heavy defilements.
I shall explain the Seal of Great Compassion to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
In the past, when I sat beneath the Bodhi tree,
I maintained this seal by means of a heart of great compassion.
All the hosts of Māras shall naturally disperse and submit to those who bind this seal.
One who binds this seal should do so while upholding it with the power of all Buddhas, the power of the Dharma, the power of the Arhats, and the power of the mind of loving-kindness.
Then, one obtains the seal-mantra for the swift eradication of all extremely heavy karmic stains and defilements.
The mantra is as follows: Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | tadyathā | kuṃkuni ni | oṃ kurumārañjare | prakhase prakhase maṃ hūṃ | kumārīśriye | marīci nūke | svāhā || This is the seal-mantra.
This is called the "Dhāraṇī of the Tathāgata’s Great Compassionate Power.
If there is one who recites this dhāraṇī,
they should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness while upholding it.
Then, by the power of this seal and mantra, one shall not be afflicted by any *vināyakas*,
tigers, wolves, enemies, or bandits, nor by quarrels, strife, calamities,
or sudden disturbances.
Because one swiftly realizes the samādhi of the compassionate mind,
the forty-eight seals of the Tathāgata’s great compassion are formed by joining the two hands in *añjali*.
With the palms hollowed,
bend the two thumbs into the palms;
the mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namo samanta-buddhānām | Oṃ hūṃ taṭa luṅ phaṭ ṅe ṅe naṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā | This seal-mantra is named the Gate of the Tathāgata’s Great Compassion Samādhi.
The Forty-Ninth Seal of the Tathāgata’s Stainless Seal: Following the previous Compassion Seal, change the tip of the ring finger.
Press down beneath the thumb;
next, use the tip of the little finger.
Pressing the thumb against the nail, the mantra is recited as follows:
Namo bhagavate vajrapāṇaye hūṃ māradaṃṣṭriṇe hulu hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the seal-mantra.
The wise person should constantly recite mantras over all food and drink;
by consuming and partaking of them while maintaining this practice, one can extinguish all sins.
Furthermore, one shall not be harmed or afflicted by Vināyakas within one's food.
The Fifty Mudrās of the Tathāgata’s Amṛta: Furthermore, with the right thumb, one presses across the tips of the index, middle, ring, and little fingers; the mudrā-mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām | Oṃ hūṃ | Indriṇi indriṇi | Svāhā || This one-seal mantra enables the practitioner who upholds it.
The Seal of the Great Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata, the Great Gate of Liberation for Realizing the Dharma of Ambrosia, No. 51: Join the palms at the heart.
With the thumbs of both the left and right hands,
each bend [the thumb] within the palm.
Furthermore, with the two index fingers, two middle fingers, two ring fingers, and two little fingers of each hand, bend and grasp the thumbs to form fists.
The thumbs are placed back-to-back.
The eight fingers should not touch the palms. The mantra is recited as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ hūṃ kara-karabha-raja-ti-ra huṃ phaṭ*. This seal and mantra are named "The Great Lion’s Roar."
One accomplishes the teachings of the Vajraśekhara-cakravartin.

Because it can extensively demonstrate inconceivable, unprecedented, and super-mundane matters that transcend the intellect, there are fifty-two *tathāgata-lakṣaṇākṣara-mudrās* for the fifty-two *tathāgata-lakṣaṇākṣara-mudrās*. Furthermore, with the eight fingers of the left and right hands—
Each hand is extended and opened;
the right hand presses down upon the left,
with the fingers interlaced and the middle joints pressed together.
The tips of the eight fingers should each be extended straight upward,
without touching the gaps between them.
As for the two thumbs:
Each [hand] is likewise held with fingers splayed diagonally and extended upward,
the heads of the thumbs being one and a half inches apart.
Placing the seal at a distance of three inches from the chest, the mantra for the seal is recited as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām. This one-seal mantra is named the Tathāgata-Mahāpuruṣa-Lakṣaṇa-Samādhi-dvāra.
The fifty-third is the Tathāgata-lakṣmī-śrī-mudrā; furthermore, with the left and right hands...
The arms are joined together;
the ten fingers are each splayed open,
held straight upward, slightly extended and bent.
The heads [of the fingers] are each separated by one and a half inches.
This is the mudrā of the Opening Lotus; the mantra is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ hūṃ sumbha niṣumbha lokeśmi lokeśmi svāhā*. This mudrā and mantra are called the Tathāgata-Śrī-Samādhi-mukha.
It enables the holder to obtain the great wealth of the Dharma and be honored and praised by all people.
This is the fifty-fourth seal of the Tathāgata’s Prajñāpāramitā; it is also known as the Seal of Offering. Furthermore, one joins the two hands in *añjali*.
Hollowed within the palms like an unopened lotus bud.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ hūṃ śruti seṭi mṛtyu-mṛtyaye svāhā. This is the mantra of the seal of Guhyapati.
It is called the Tathāgata’s Gate of Samādhi of Prajñāpāramitā.
All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, as well as all great Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and so forth, [rely upon it].
All arise from this seal-mantra samādhi-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā;
they thereby realize and attain the stage of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus one knows that this seal-mantra possesses great majestic power and virtue.
She is named the Mother of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, of all Great Bodhisattvas, of all Vajradharas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secret Traces, saying:
These mudrās and mantras arise from the major and minor marks that adorn the bodies and limbs of all Tathāgatas,
O son of good family. Furthermore, the Tathāgatas possess immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of mantras and mudrās.
Each of these individual seals has its own immeasurable retinue of seals and so forth,
which together constitute this King of Mantras, the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakra-vartin.
I now briefly explain a small portion of these seals and mantras for the sake of those who shall accomplish this incantation in future ages, so that they may obtain great benefit.
Guhya-pati, in future times,
there will be few sentient beings who can understand the ritual application of these mantra-seals.
You should read, recite, and uphold these mantra-seals according to the dharma.
For the sake of all sentient beings in future ages,
I shall provide a detailed explanation;
this is due to the power and efficacy of the mudrās and mantras of the attendants of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.
If a son of good family wishes to accomplish this Great One-Syllable Cakravartin King Mantra,
he should always maintain purity and constantly recite this mantra-wheel while binding this mudrā.
Such a person shall obtain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of praiseworthy merits.
All darkness, defilements, and obscurations are extinguished;
one is joyfully regarded and compassionately favored by all Tathāgatas and great Bodhisattvas;
and in every place of rebirth, one attains the knowledge of past lives.
Their physical marks, mental faculties, and wisdom shall all be perfected;
they shall be free from premature death and illness,
and shall be able to act as a great light for sentient beings.
They are able to deliver sentient beings from evil realms;
they attain great eloquence and wisdom, possess great diligence,
and are endowed with radiant majesty and a perfect retinue.
He thoroughly understands all the arts and crafts of the world and is able to cure and rescue all sentient beings from the diseases of affliction and ignorance.
He is constantly sustained by the empowerment and mindful protection of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
One will presently attain the pure Dharma-body of a bodhisattva.
If there should be anyone who daily and constantly performs the mudrās and recites these mantras while calling their own name, [they shall achieve this].
Then one shall not be oppressed, terrified, or afflicted by any *vināyakas*,
and all karmic obstructions will naturally be extinguished.
If one realizes this Great One-Syllable Cakravartin King Mantra in this very life, [the following shall occur].
For this reason, in future ages, one will certainly attain the Great Samādhi of the Buddha’s Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment.
Lord Guhyapati, these mudrās and mantras are the true Dharma-torches of the mudrās and mantras of the lineage of all Tathāgatas.
Now, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, in order to bring to fulfillment those who practice the mantra of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin,
has spoken this seal-mantra and samādhi-gate.
*The Scripture of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin*, Fascicle Three.

The Scripture of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin, Scroll Four, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Chapter Eight: The Great Dharma Mandala. **Chapter Eight: The Great Dharma Mandala** [The Buddha] addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas: "If there are those who wish to attain the supreme fruit of Buddhahood, they must first construct a great dharma mandala. Regarding this great dharma mandala, one should select a site that is level, pure, and free from impurities. It should be situated where the ground is firm and the location is auspicious. Having selected such a place, one should clear away all weeds and thorns, and smear the ground with cow dung and fragrant mud.

Then, one should draw the great dharma mandala according to the prescribed measurements and proportions. Within the mandala, one should arrange the various implements and offerings, including flowers, incense, lamps, and food. Furthermore, one should invite the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, and with a mind of profound faith and reverence, perform the rites of worship and praise. By doing so, one will swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression and ultimately realize the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of a Buddha. Thus spoke the Buddha. At that time, the entire assembly, having heard these words, rejoiced and put them into practice. Thus ends the eighth chapter of the *Ekākṣaroṣṇīṣacakravartin-sūtra*, titled "The Great Dharma Mandala."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secret Traces, saying:
"Listen attentively;
for the benefit of all sentient beings, I shall [speak]."
This is a brief explanation of the Great Secret Maṇḍala of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakra King.
This maṇḍala [prevails] throughout both the supramundane and the mundane.
It is the most supreme and the highest.
Just as, among the thirty-two marks of a Great Man belonging to a Tathāgata, the mark of the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa) is the most supreme;
and just as the Tathāgata is the great teacher among gods and humans.
This Great Maṇḍala of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa King is likewise so;
among all mantra maṇḍalas, it is the supreme Great Wheel-King,
capable of extinguishing all inauspicious signs.
It is capable of subduing all evil devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, and other sentient beings;
it is capable of bestowing [benefits] upon all who study the Mahāyāna.
It purifies all defilements of sin and realizes all supreme meritorious deeds as the gateway to Great Nirvāṇa.
When constructing the maṇḍala:
Whenever one awaits the first, eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the white fortnight, or any auspicious constellation,
date, and time, at the break of dawn,
one should bathe in scented water and don fresh, clean garments.
Before a stūpa containing relics, or in the mountains,
or to the east or north of a town,
one should seek out a secluded and pure place by the side of a spring, a pond, or a river.
One should select an excellent site,
measuring thirty-two cubits, or sixteen cubits, or twelve cubits, or again eight cubits,
according to the required number of cubits.
First, sweep and clean the area.
Then, the Ācārya, holding a vajra,
stands facing east at the center of the mandala site.
He asked his disciples,
"Do you all resolutely seek to study the secret Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas?
Do you harbor no doubts?"
Then the disciples all answered at once:
"We, [Name] and the others, are resolved to study the profound Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas;
with absolute certainty and sincere faith, we give rise to no doubt."
When these three questions and three answers were thus concluded,
the ācārya again consecrated the incense burner with mantra and mudrā, held it,
knelt long on his knees facing east, and burned the incense while reciting the mantra.
I prostrate to all Buddhas of the ten directions,
to all Bodhisattvas of the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin,
and to all Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, nāgas, and spirits.
And all the paths of karma, as well as all the deities and spirits,
bear witness and know that I now request this ground as my own territory.
Upon this ground, I shall establish for seven days and seven nights the dharma assembly of the Great Maṇḍala of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakra King,
making offerings to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, the Sugatas, throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm.
This profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the treasury of all secret and profound dharmas, an inconceivable gateway to the Dharma,
[is attended by] all the great bodhisattvas, all the vajra deities, and their respective retinues.
I request you to bear witness to my accomplishment.
I wish to perform the ritual for protecting the body and binding the boundaries within this location,
in the four cardinal directions— east, south, west, and north— as well as the four intermediate directions and above and below.
All *vināyakas*, evil spirits, ghosts, and others who destroy the Buddha-dharma,
shall all depart to a distance of seven *li*.
As for the benevolent gods, spirits, and others who protect the Buddha-dharma...
Those who act for the benefit of the Buddha-dharma should remain settled as appropriate;
having performed the three "white" offerings (*triśukla*), they should then bind the heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*) of the Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣavijaya-rāja,
protect themselves, and recite the Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣavijaya-mantra that shatters [obstacles].
Recite the mantra over white mustard seeds and scented water seven times,
then scatter them in the ten directions to seal and demarcate the boundaries of the ritual altar.
Thereafter, one may determine the dimensions of the square or circle according to the number of cubits;
then, one should excavate and remove the inferior soil,
tiles, stones, roots, wood, bones, grass, and all other such deleterious objects.
The pit shall be one cubit deep;
fill it with pure, high-quality earth and compact it firmly until level,
then raise a foundation half a cubit high.
On the northeastern side of the altar, let the base be slightly lower.
At each of the four corners and at the center of the altar,
pierce a small circular hole.
It should be dug to a depth of half a cubit.
Within it, bury the seven treasures, the five grains, and other such items.
As for those seven treasures:

First, gold; second, silver; third, pearls; fourth, coral; fifth, amber; sixth, *sphaṭika* (translated into Chinese as "resembling crystal," though its specific nature is not fully known); seventh, lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*).
As for the five grains:
first, barley; second, wheat; third, rice; fourth, small beans; and fifth, sesame.
As for the fragments of the seven treasures:
Take equal portions, like beans,
of the five grains, one *he* each,
and divide them with clean white silk.
Wrap it together and hold it;
recite the mantra seven times and tie it at the head with thread of five colors.
Bury it within the five holes,
leaving the end of the thread protruding from the surface of the ground to a length of five finger-widths.
Once it has been buried, it shall never again be permitted to be unearthed and removed.
Level it according to the Dharma,
using fresh, pure *gomaya* mixed with yellow and white earth,
and well-kneaded clay perfumed with scented water.
Rotate it daily according to the ritual, adorn it with ointments as prescribed,
and further consecrate the outer boundary of the mandala by reciting mantras over scattered white mustard seeds.
From the northeast corner to the southeast corner,
and likewise from the southwest corner to the northwest corner,
erect a pole at each location, all twelve feet in length, regardless of whether they are made of bamboo or wood. Furthermore, from the pole at the northeast corner, measure upward one foot.
Tie it to the top of the staff and lead it to the triangular point;
do likewise until it has reached the northeast corner and the circuit is complete.
Then, from the northeast corner,
various divine banners, silk streamers, flower garlands, bells, and ribbons were suspended in an alternating array;
golden and silver lotuses were spread everywhere as adornments.
Outside the boundary of sixteen cubits, on each of the four sides,
measure out an area of four feet square;
then, according to the Dharma, prepare the ground, tie the cord, and demarcate the boundary.
Having established the ritual procedures for practicing the Way,
one further binds the mudrā to protect the body and enters the maṇḍala,
reciting the mantra of the Cakravartin King Crusher.
Recite the mantra over white mustard seeds and over the ashes from burnt fire-offerings one hundred and eight times.
Next, recite the Heart Mantra of Sarvārthasiddhi-cakravartin.
The number of white mustard seeds, ashes, and so forth should also be as stated above.
One should then hold these white mustard seeds and ashes.
Turning to the right from the northeast corner of the altar,
recite the mantra while circling it completely,
scattering [the offerings] in the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Bind the boundaries of the pure mandala.
Furthermore, recite the Vajra-vidāraṇa Uṣṇīṣarāja mantra over four stakes made of khadira wood, each nine inches in length.
Recite one hundred and eight times.
Next, recite the heart-mantra of Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣavijaya.
As previously done with the mantra-nails, [perform the same here].
Starting from the northeast corner, recite the mantra once for each time you drive in a ritual stake, continuing until seven sets of seven have been completed.
The method for driving stakes in the remaining three corners and so forth is likewise the same.
Furthermore, sit on your knees with the body extended toward the west.
Recite the mantra over asitagarbha incense and aloeswood seven times and burn them.
Form the Buddhacakṣus mudrā and recite the Buddhacakṣus mantra;
seal the incense burner with the mudrā and mantra seven times.
Holding a censer in his hand, he further spoke these words:
"I, [Name], now address all Buddhas of the ten directions and all Prajñāpāramitās."
All the Bodhisattvas of the Uṣṇīṣarāja,
all the Bodhisattvas of Avalokiteśvara,
and all the great Bodhisattvas.
May all the Bodhisattvas Vajragarbha and the rest,
and all the gods, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings— those divine kings who protect the stūpas and the Dharma—
bear witness to me, the bhikṣu [Name].
Having performed the Great Samaya Mandala for the Consecration of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin,
and having requested the King of Dharma’s grace and the fulfillment of his merits and aspirations, he spoke these words.
Furthermore, starting from the northeast corner of the maṇḍala,
one proceeds clockwise around the perimeter to form the *vajra* seal of the diligence of the heart-essence of all Tathāgatas.
The mudrā of the King of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa;
the mudrā of Turning the Wheel of Dharma;
and the heart-mudrā of all Uṣṇīṣa Kings.
The seal of the Tathāgata’s eye;
the seal of the Invincible Wrathful King;
the seal of the Cakravartin who shatters [all things].
Thus, with these seven seals,
one performs the sequential wheel-binding in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below,
thereby establishing the square boundaries of the maṇḍala.
Furthermore, one should be established facing east at the center of the mandala,
using the heart-seal of Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣarāja and the seal of Vajroṣṇīṣa that shatters all [obstacles].
At a height of one cubit above the crown of the head,
turn three times clockwise and stamp the ground;
this is called binding the great boundary of the upper and lower directions.
Furthermore, perform the rite of the *kuntali-vajra* boundary-binding once.
This method of boundary-binding is called the *Mahāsamādhi Boundary-Binding Rite of the Consecration Altar of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin*.
Thereafter, exit the mandala together with the painters and one disciple who has previously entered the mandala and received the transmission of the Dharma.
Forming mudrās to protect the body, recite as follows:
Take this five-colored cord and follow me into the maṇḍala,
circling from the northeast toward the southwest.
The dimensions of the arm-span altar site are divided into four courtyards by inner and outer streets,
with only the western gate opened.
The inner sanctum is divided;
it is four cubits square in total and comprises thirteen partitions.
The central partition is two cubits square.
In the center is painted Śākyamuni Tathāgata,
facing west with eyes blinking, seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
He assumes the gesture of preaching the Dharma (*dharmacakra-mudrā*) while seated upon a precious lion throne atop a jeweled lotus flower.
From the crown of his head, he emits great rays of light.
To the right of the Buddha,
one should paint the Bodhisattva Ekākṣarocchusma Cakravartin.
Beholding the Tathāgata seated in the half-lotus posture,
his left hand holding an opened lotus flower;
upon the calyx of the flower, a golden wheel made of the seven treasures is depicted standing upright at a slight angle.
Surrounding the wheel’s razor-sharp blades,
draw great flames;
the right hand has its palm raised.
To the left of the Buddha, depict the Venerable Subhūti standing;
to the right of the Buddha, depict the Venerable Ānanda standing.
Divide the four sides into twelve panels.
To the right and north of the Buddha, one should paint the Bodhisattva Vajra-āśani-kleśarāja.
With his right hand at his chest, he holds an open lotus flower;
upon the calyx of the flower, a single-pronged vajra is depicted vertically.
The right hand is raised with the palm facing outward at the side of the chest.
To the south of the Buddha, separated by a space, is painted the Bodhisattva Tejorāśi-uṣṇīṣacakravartin;
his left hand holds an open lotus flower at the side of the chest.
Upon the flower pedestal, draw the Buddha’s heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*):
with the right hand at the side of the chest,
extend the thumb and index finger straight upward.
The middle, ring, and little fingers are bent inward toward the palm.
Next, to the east of the Vighnarāja Bodhisattva, one should paint the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin Bodhisattva.
The left hand is bent upward, grasping an open lotus flower;
upon the center of the flower’s pedestal, an eight-spoked golden wheel is drawn standing upright on its side.
The right hand is raised with the palm facing outward at the level of the chest.
Next, on the eastern partition of the Bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna-uṣṇīṣarāja,
paint the Bodhisattva Sitātapatrā-uṣṇīṣarāja.
His left hand is bent upward, grasping an opened lotus flower.
On the flower pedestal, draw a parasol.
With his right hand at his chest, he holds an opened lotus.
Next, to the west of the Buddha, facing south, is the space.
Draw a square circle measuring one chi and two cun with a precious wheel of eight spokes;
around the rim of the wheel, draw flames all along the edges.
Next, in the northern partition, paint the Bodhisattva Uṣṇīṣavijayā.
With the left hand held against the chest, one grasps an open lotus flower.
Upon the center of the flower, draw a vertical sword;
around the edge of the sword blade, draw great flames.
His right hand is bent outward, grasping a blue utpala lotus.
Next, in the northeast, separated by a partition, is painted the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī;
his left hand is at the side of his chest, grasping a blue utpala lotus.
The right hand is bent upward with the palm turned inward.
Next, to the south of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
paint Sarvārthasiddhi Bodhisattva.
With the left hand at the side of the abdomen, he grasps and opens a lotus flower;
upon the calyx of the flower, five-colored conch shells are drawn vertically.
With the right hand at the side of the chest, the palm is raised upward.
In the northeast corner, separated by a partition,
is depicted the Bodhisattva Trailokyavijaya (Cui-sui-ding-lun-wang).
With his left hand at his chest, he holds an opened lotus flower.
On the flower pedestal, draw a vajra-bannered pennant.
The right hand is bent upward with the palm facing inward and raised.
To the left, draw the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā.
With the left hand, one should hold open a lotus flower at the breast;
upon the calyx of the flower, draw the Buddha-heart seal (hṛdaya-mudrā),
with a single eye drawn on each side of the seal.
The right hand is bent upward with the palm facing inward and raised;
in the southeast corner, separated by a barrier,
paint the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra Trilokavijaya.
The left hand is held at the chest, opening a lotus flower;
upon the calyx of the flower, a vajra is drawn upright.
The right hand is held at the chest with the palm facing outward and raised.
To the right, depict the Bodhisattva Ūrṇākośa (Hair-Treasure).
With his left hand, he holds an opened lotus flower level with his breast;
upon the calyx of the flower, depict the seal of the Buddha’s hair-treasure (*ūrṇā-kośa-mudrā*).
Form a fist by hollowly bending the four fingers of the right hand;
extend the thumb straight and press it against the side of the right ribcage at the southwest corner.
In the painting, depict the Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddhi-Uṣṇīṣacakravartin:
with his left hand extended upward, he grasps and opens a lotus flower upon his left thigh;
his right hand is held at the chest in an upward-facing fist, with the four fingers curled and the thumb extended straight.
To the right, depict the Bodhisattva Śūla;
his right hand holds a spear,
beneath the tip of which a hanging silk ribbon is drawn.
With the left hand slightly bent, the four fingers are pressed against the upper side of the abdomen;
in the northwest corner, partitioned off,
paint the Bodhisattva Holy Aparimitāyurjñāna-cakravartin.
The left hand is inverted and bent, grasping the side of the left flank while opening a lotus flower;
upon the calyx of the flower, a jeweled conch is drawn upright.
The right hand is positioned at the side of the breast, with the palm raised upward.
To the right is painted the Bodhisattva Dantadhāraṇī.
She extends her left hand, placing it upon her left thigh and grasping an open lotus flower.
Upon the calyx of the flower, the seal (mudrā) of the Tathāgata’s tooth is painted.
The right hand is held at the chest in an empty fist with the four fingers closed and the thumb extended straight;
the bodily radiance and physical characteristics of these bodhisattvas are as previously described.
Each was adorned with flower crowns, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and various garments;
they wore a pervasive light throughout their bodies and sat in the half-lotus posture upon lotus seats.
The second courtyard is divided;
it should be two cubits wide,
with twenty-four partitions distributed across its four sides.
In the first bay to the south of the northeast corner,
depict the Tathāgata Ratnolkā of the East;
his left hand is turned downward at the level of his chest, grasping the corner of his *kāṣāya*.
With his right hand raised in the gesture of the open palm,
he faces the second panel to the south, where Akṣobhya Tathāgata of the north is depicted;
his left hand is extended upward below the navel, grasping the corner of his *kāṣāya*.
With the right hand extended palm-downward placed upon the right thigh in the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudrā).
In the third bay to the south,
paint the Tathāgata Amitābha of the western direction.
Press the back of the left hand over the palm of the right hand and extend them downward to rest below the navel.
To the south, in the fourth compartment, is depicted the Tathāgata King of the Fully Blossomed Lotus of the South.
Extend the left hand downward below the navel to grasp the corner of the *kāṣāya*.
The right hand is bent upward with the palm facing up and extended;
in the fifth bay to the south,
paint the heart-seal (hṛdaya-mudrā) of all Buddhas.
Surrounded by blazing flames,
these four Buddhas possess golden-colored bodies and are adorned with light radiating from their entire forms.
Seated in the full lotus posture upon a lion throne of precious lotuses,
in the first bay to the east of the northwest corner facing north,
one should paint the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī.
The face has three eyes and the body has four arms;
one hand holds a lotus flower,
and the other hand holds a kunda.
Holding a rosary in one hand,
with the other extended upward toward the navel;
on the right, two attendants are depicted.
Each sits with legs extended in a kneeling posture upon a lotus seat.
Holding a handful of flowers, they scatter them.
On the second partition to the east, one paints the Bodhisattva Tārā.
The left hand is held with the palm facing upward, extended horizontally below the navel, grasping a blue *utpala* flower;
the right hand is bent upward with the palm facing up.
To the right, paint two attendant bodhisattvas.
Both [deities] join their palms and kneel with long legs, seated upon lotus-leaf seats.
In the third bay to the east,
paint the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The left hand holds a lotus flower against the chest;
the right hand is extended upward below the navel.
Furthermore, paint the Mother of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara in White Robes.
The left hand grasps an opened lotus flower;
the right hand extends below the navel.
This is the fourth enclosure in the east.
He painted the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta with his left hand grasping a half-open lotus flower below the navel,
and his right hand held at the chest with the palm turned upward and slightly extended.
To the right is depicted the Bodhisattva Mahāśvetā.
Her left hand is palm upturned upon her left thigh, grasping a lotus flower;
her right hand makes the gesture of stroking the crown of the head.
In the fifth bay on the east wall,
there is a depiction of Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
His left hand is held at his chest, grasping a battle-axe.
In his right hand he holds a lotus, a water lily, and so forth;
to the right is painted the Bodhisattva Mahāśrī.
In his left hand, pressed against his navel, he holds an open lotus.
Their right hands are extended upward and placed upon their right thighs.
The bodily radiance and fleshly complexion of these Bodhisattvas are as previously described;
each is adorned with flower crowns, necklaces, and bracelets.
Adorned with various garments,
he sits upon a lotus throne in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka),
facing south, in the first bay to the west of the southeast corner.
Paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
his left hand holds a vajra at the side of his chest,
and his right hand has its palm raised.
To the right is depicted the Bodhisattva Vajravārāhī;
her left hand holds a vajra at her chest,
while her right palm is turned upward with the fingers extended below her navel.
To the right is painted the Bodhisattva Kīlikīla-vajra;
his left hand holds a vajra at his chest,
while his right hand is raised with the palm facing outward.
In the second partition on the west is the Bodhisattva born of the Vajra family.
He presses the back of his right hand against the palm of his left hand, extending them downward below the navel, with a vajra held in his palms.
To the right is depicted the youth Vajrakumāra Sūkṣma;
his left hand holds a vajra-mallet obliquely against his chest,
while his right hand rests upon his right thigh.
In the third compartment to the west is the Bodhisattva Vajrapiṭaka, depicted in a state of fierce wrath.
His face is full of anger;
with his right hand, he grasps a vajra at a slant against his chest.
The left hand is bent upward, grasping a three-pronged trident;
to the right is painted the youth Krodha-Ḍākinīvajra,
his left hand held askew at the chest, clutching a vajra.
His right hand holds a three-pronged trident.
In the fourth bay to the west,
depict the Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi.
The left hand is held against the chest in the *vajramuṣṭi-mudrā*;
the right hand is palm upturned and placed upon the right thigh.
To the right, one should depict the youth Vajra-subāhu.
On the head, a vajra-head is depicted;
with both arms crossed at the elbows, each hand grasps a vajra.
This is the fifth section from the west.
Depict the Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśī holding a vajra-hook.
Her left hand is held at her chest in the gesture of grasping the vajra-hook (vajrāṅkuśa-mudrā);
her right hand is palm upturned, resting upon her right thigh.
To the right is depicted the Bodhisattva Vajrasphoṭa.
His left hand is held at the chest in the vajra-chain mudrā,
while his right hand is extended upward below the navel.
To the right, depict the Vajrakumāra Mucilinda;
his left hand grasps a vajra,
and his right hand is held at the chest with the palm turned upward and slightly extended.
The color and appearance of these vajra-bodies are as previously described;
each is adorned according to the ritual rules with flower crowns, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and various garments.
All are seated in the half-lotus posture upon lotus thrones.
In the first bay to the north, separating the southwest corner from the west side,
one should paint the Bodhisattva Trailokyavijaya.
His face has three eyes and canine fangs protruding upward; his countenance is one of great fury.
His left hand, held against his chest, clutches a vajra askew, while his right hand rests upon a long sword.
To the right is depicted the messenger Acala,
his face wrathful;
with his left hand he grasps a noose.
His right hand is held obliquely upright against his chest, grasping a sword.
In the second bay to the north is depicted Maitreya Bodhisattva,
holding a lotus flower in his left hand.
On the flower pedestal, draw a water jar;
the right hand is raised with the palm facing outward.
To the right, draw the deity Mahāpratyaṅgirā, the Great Wrathful King.
His face was filled with great rage;
his left hand was held across his chest, grasping a vajra at an angle,
while his right hand held a sword, poised in a threatening gesture.
In the first bay of the northern gate,
depict the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrīkumāra;
his left hand holds a blossoming lotus flower at his chest.
On the flower pedestal, draw a three-pronged vajra.
The right hand is bent upward with the palm facing outward.
To the left, draw two attendants.
The first is named Kṣapaṇīśvarī Bodhisattva;
the second is named Kṣaṇī Bodhisattva.
One holds a spear, and the other holds a sword.
All hold [the objects] in their right hands.
Next, in the second partition to the north of the gate,
paint the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
The right hand is held obliquely upright at the chest grasping a sword;
the left hand is bent outward with the palm facing upward.
To the right, one should paint the *śivamukha* vidyārājñī.
Standing with an angry posture, he extends his left hand to form the *bhṛkuṭī* gesture with force;
his right hand is held at the chest, yellowish-white in color.
These Bodhisattvas are adorned with light radiating from their entire bodies.
Their physical forms are as previously described;
each is adorned with flower crowns, necklaces,
bracelets, armlets, and various garments.
All are seated in the half-lotus posture upon lotus thrones.
In the northeast corner,
one should paint the Eastern Deity Vighnāntaka.
The body is greenish-blue in color, with a wrathful expression on the face.
The right hand holds the breast,
while the left hand forms a fist pressed against the left shoulder.
On each side, paint an attendant;
one stands holding a censer,
and the other kneels with palms joined, holding a lasso.
In the southeast corner partition,
paint the Deity Who Eliminates Fear of the South;
his body is reddish-yellow in color, and his face and eyes are wrathful.
The left hand presses against the navel, held upright and cupped;
the right hand is at the chest, slightly hollowed into a fist.
To the left and right, paint one standing attendant each.
A trident and a vajra are placed in the southwest corner.
Paint the deity Aparājita of the western quarter;
his body is white-yellow in color, his face is wrathful,
and with his left hand he holds a noose at his chest.
The right hand forms a fist and rests upon the right knee.
To the right, one attendant is depicted,
sitting in a long-kneeling posture.
Holding a trident-fork,
in the northwest corner,
one should paint the Northern Deity who Dispels Fear.
The body is purple-red in color, with a face of wrathful expression.
With his right hand, he holds a sword upright and askew against his chest.
To his left and right, a standing attendant is painted in each position.
One holds a sword and one holds a wheel;
these deities of the four directions are each adorned with flower garlands, necklaces, and bracelets,
and are arrayed in various garments according to the ritual dharma.
All [deities] sit in the half-lotus posture upon lotus seats.
The third enclosure is also two cubits wide and is painted entirely with a blue ground.
The intersections of golden cords are adorned with precious flowers.
The fourth courtyard is likewise two cubits wide;
its four sides are divided into forty-two compartments.
On the eastern side, there is a partition;
paint the Śuddhāvāsa deities and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin deities.
Furthermore, having depicted all the devas and so forth,
one should paint Śakra, the King of Devas, in the southeastern section.
Paint the fire deity,
with all the celestial sages (ṛṣis) depicted as his retinue;
this is the southern sector.
Paint Nārāyaṇa,
the Dragon King Ānanda,
and King Yama.
And one should depict Hārītī with her retinue of piśāca spirits and pūtana spirits.
In the southwest,
separated by a partition, depict Mahāśrīdevī and the host of rākṣasa kings.
With the hosts of *bhūta* spirits as their retinue;
on the western side,
depict the Water Heavenly King (*Varuṇa*) together with his retinue.
On the left and right sides of the Water Deity King,
paint the Nāga King Nanda and the Nāga King Upananda as his retinue.
In the northwest direction, depict the wind deities (Vāyu-devas) separated by lines;
depict various vidyādhara sages,
as well as the hosts of kṛtya kings, as their retinue.
In the northern section,
paint the deity Maheśvara and paint the mantra-deity Mahāsenā.
The celestial maidens of the Suyāma heaven,
as well as various yakṣas and others depicted as their retinue,
are situated in the northeastern direction.
Paint Mahābrahmā,
the host of Īśvara-devas,
and the kumbhāṇḍa spirits.
Various classes of *yakṣas* serve as his retinue.
Furthermore, in the first bay to the south of the eastern gate,
paint the Sun Deity (*Sūryadeva*).
And depict the Seven Stars and their celestial hosts surrounding them in front and behind.
In the second bay to the south of the western gate,
depict the Moon Deva.
Furthermore, depict the Seven Stars and the celestial hosts surrounding them in front and behind.
Moreover, in the second partition to the north of the western gate,
depict the messenger Dṛti and the deity Piśāca.
And paint the remaining messengers as well.
Furthermore, at the eastern gate, paint the yakṣa general Pūrṇabhadra and the yakṣa general Ratnapāla.
Furthermore, at the head of the southern gate, one should paint the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka,
along with Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the other [heavenly kings].
Furthermore, the Seven Stars and their celestial hosts should be depicted, surrounded on the left and right.
Additionally, at the head of the western gate,
King Virūpākṣa should be painted.
Paint the Great Yakṣa Lord Pañcika;
furthermore, at the head of the northern gate,
paint the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
And one should depict the Seven Stars surrounded on all sides by celestial hosts;
the bodies and ornaments of these Four Heavenly Kings are as previously described.
These include various celestial sages, nāga kings, spirits, and so forth.
Each is adorned with their own respective garments and original weapons.
They all sit in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*).
The innermost first enclosure shall be two and a half inches wide.
On all four sides, surrounding the perimeter,
erect vajras are drawn with their tips touching one another;
upon each vajra, flames are drawn everywhere.
The boundary of the second courtyard is likewise two and a half inches wide;
all four sides are painted with paths of the seven treasures.
The boundary of the third courtyard outside should be three inches wide.
On all four sides, surrounding the perimeter, vajra-wands are drawn standing upright with their tips touching one another;
this is done across every single vajra-wand.
Paint a great mass of flames.
The boundary of the fourth enclosure should be four inches wide.
On all four sides, paint the paths of the seven precious jewels as a boundary.
The boundary of the fifth outer enclosure should be six inches wide;
all around its four sides, vajra-wheels are to be drawn standing upright,
their tips touching one another.
Furthermore, one should draw great tongues of fire upon each and every vajra.
The ground of both the inner and outer enclosures is to be smeared entirely with blue.
On each of the four sides of the altar, both the inner and outer gates,
as well as the southern gate, shall each open to one side,
so that the mantra-practitioner may enter and exit and move about freely.
Thus, one should draw the maṇḍala either on silk or on fine cloth,
measuring one cubit (*hasta*) and following the prescribed ritual rules.
The artisan must bathe daily to cleanse himself and wear fresh, clean garments.
Having received the three-refuge precepts, one should blend pigments with white mustard seeds and,
according to the ritual,
apply the colors while reciting the heart-mantra of Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣavijaya over the pigments.
Furthermore, one should hold incense, flowers, food and drink, scented water, and other articles of offering,
and offer them after consecrating them with mantras.
If a painted image has been made, then one should use the root-heart seal and mantra of Sarvatathāgata-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin.
Recite the mantra of the Cakravartin Seal of Destruction over white mustard seeds seventeen times for each seal. Then,
circumambulate clockwise around the inner and outer courtyards while scattering them.
Having established the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) of the square altar and its four intermediate directions,
one should further place a large, precious, multicolored parasol upon the altar.
Within that, at the four corners outside the third enclosure:
Following the previous ritual procedure, erect poles and attach ropes; however,
suspend and arrange in an alternating pattern on all four sides banners of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, along with exquisite colored silks, flowers, bells, ribbons, pearls,
and pendants to create a magnificent adornment.
At each of its four gates and four corners,
a pair of vajra banners is suspended in opposition.
Outside, at the four gates and four corners of the fifth enclosure:
Furthermore, banners for the Four Heavenly Kings and banners for various spirit-kings were suspended individually;
above the four directions of both the inner and outer courtyards,
new large banners were hung around the perimeter to form a border.
In the four directions of the outer enclosure below,
spread new, clean woolen rugs, mats, and the like everywhere.
Within the inner enclosure, before Śākyamuni Buddha, [arrange the seats].
Place one jar of fragrant water at the center.
Place one jar of fragrant water at each of the four corners both inside and outside.
Furthermore, place two jars of fragrant water opposite each other at each of the four gates of both the inner and outer courtyards.
The incense jars and so forth each have a capacity of one *dou*.
Within each jar, place five kinds of grain seeds and fragments of the seven precious gems,
and fill them completely with scented water.
It is as if all manner of flower branches and leaves were inserted into one's mouth.
Upon the boundary lines of the four sides of both the inner and outer enclosures,
two hundred multicolored glass bubble-flowers and flowers of mixed gold and silver are scattered.
Furthermore, there were four silver trays:
one filled with burning incense and one filled with flowers.
One vessel should contain white mustard seeds, small stones, and the like;
another should contain various powdered incenses.
These should be placed on both sides of the western gate of the outer enclosure.
In the three inner and outer courtyards, at the four gates and four corners,
place incense burners and burn various kinds of famous incense.
At that time, whenever the practitioner wishes to form mudrās, recite mantras, and perform invocations, [he should do so].
One must wash the hands and rinse the mouth; furthermore, one should recite mantras over scented water and white mustard seeds, sprinkling them while circling to the right.
Forming the mudrā to protect the body, one kneels at the western gate.
Furthermore, recite the mantra over the incense burner seven times.
Holding the incense burner in hand, address it once more, saying:
"I, [Name], now make this offering to all Buddhas of the ten directions."
The Five-Crested Wheel-Turning King,
the inconceivable Dharma-gate of the entire, profound, and boundless treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā,
and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,
Maitreya Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
and Vajrapāṇi Guhyapati Bodhisattva.
All the great bodhisattvas, the assembly of bodhisattvas of all vajra families,
the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, the various virtuous spirit-kings who protect the stupas and the Dharma, and all the messengers.
I now invite you all to descend and bear witness as I, [Name], perform the ritual of the maṇḍala for the dhāraṇī of the Samādhi of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa;
may this supreme merit be accomplished according to my wish.
Having thus requested the bestowal of blessings three times, one should then form the seal of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King,
which is the heart-seal of all Cakravartin Kings and the seal of the Destroyer of All Cakravartin Kings.
In all cases, one should seal [the body] with reverence while wearing the crown upon the head;
then, using the seal and mantra of the *Cūḍāmaṇi-vajrapāṇi* (Crown-Wheel King),
seal seven times the left shoulder, right shoulder, throat, heart, the upper part of the chest, the left and right knees, the space between the eyebrows, and the hairline.
Then, seal the crown of the head and the area behind the crown;
sealing these locations three times each is called "binding the boundary of the body."
The methods for protecting one's companions and protecting one's disciples are also to be conducted according to this rule.
Then, with the thumb and middle finger of the right hand,
hold and manipulate the prayer beads.
With the left hand holding a vajra,
place white mustard seeds within a silver plate and recite the heart mantra of Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣavijaya.
Having recited the mantra of the Cakravartin King of Destruction one hundred and eight times for each,
he returns the rosary and the vajra and places them upon the silver platter.
Furthermore, bind the seal of the Cakravartin King who Shatters and Crushes.
Recite it seven times over white mustard seeds, small pebbles, and so forth.
Next, bind the seal of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.
Seal the white mustard seeds, small pebbles, and so forth, also seven times each.
Next, form the heart-seal of Sarvavid Vairocana (Sarvatathāgata-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin).
As with the previous seal, [seal] the white mustard seeds and small pebbles.
Then, holding a silver tray of mustard seeds,
one proceeds from the northeast corner within the ritual enclosure and scatters white mustard seeds while circling to the right.
Having thus completed the ritual scattering in all directions— around the perimeter, the four intermediate points, above, and below—
one takes the pebbles from the northeast corner of the outer enclosure of the mandala.
He threw a stone.
In this manner, he threw one stone each toward the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
The area reached by the stones was designated as the outer boundary.
Sprinkle mustard seeds everywhere, naming this the "inner realm.
Then, re-entering the mandala, form the *Cūḍāmaṇi-vajrapāṇi* (Crushing-Crown-Wheel-King) mudrā;
seal the ground of the mandala and recite the mantra seven times.
This is called the boundary of the earth.
With the four corners and four sides, one seals the space;
turning to the right seven times, one recites the mantra seven times.
This is called the Great Maṇḍala Boundary of the Eight Directions.
Upon entering the center of the maṇḍala, one again forms the mudrā;
at a distance of one cubit above the head, one turns to the right seven times while reciting the mantra seven times.

This concludes the rite for binding the boundary of the upper realm of space with the *muṣṭi-vajra* (vajra-fist) mudrā, as well as the method for establishing the boundary with *krodhavajra* (wrathful vajra).
Furthermore, having burned incense at the four corners and four gates:
Then, one should invoke and invite according to the Dharma and seal it with the Buddha-seal:
interlace the two ring fingers and the two little fingers of both hands, placing the right over the left within the palms.
Straighten the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another.
Extend the two index fingers straight apart at a distance of four and a half inches.
Place both thumbs upright, eight *fen* away from the middle fingers.
Recite the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.
Upon reaching the fourth repetition, gradually bend the two index fingers into the palms.
When the mantra has been completed seven times, perform the hand gesture (mudrā) and prostrate with the head in homage.
Disperse the mudrā inwardly.
By the power of this seal, one is able to summon all Tathāgatas.
This is the Lotus Throne Welcoming Seal: join the two little fingers upright and touching.
The two thumbs are likewise held upright and pressed together;
the remaining six fingers are spread evenly apart,
extended upward and slightly curved in the shape of a crescent moon.
It resembles an opening lotus flower.
Recite the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King seven times over the course of one week;
then, simultaneously bend both thumbs inward toward the palms.
Prostrate to welcome them.
Perform the mudrā for scattering toward the interior.
The mudrā for requesting them to sit: with the five fingers of the right hand.
Hold the thumbs upright and press them together.
With the index, middle, and ring fingers of the left hand,
grasp the five fingers of the right hand.
Press the thumb against the nail,
extend the little finger straight,
and recite the heart mantra of the Sarvavajroṣṇīṣarāja seven times.
Please be seated upon the throne.
Disperse the mudrās of sitting.
Request Śākyamuni Buddha to take his seat at the central position of the altar.
Next, invite the One-Syllable Cakravartin King, also according to the previous ritual method.
Next, starting from the northern end of the eastern row,
invite [the deities] one by one until reaching the southern end position.
The procedure for exhausting [the offerings] is also according to the previous method.
Next, proceed from the north to the first invitation at the western end, continuing until the positions at the eastern end;
the procedure for exhausting [the offerings] is also according to the previous method.
Next, proceed from the south along the eastern end, inviting the first seat;
continue this until the final seat at the western end, following the same procedure as before.
Next, proceed from the west along the southern end, inviting the first seat.
This continues until the end of the northern section, where the ritual procedure is likewise according to what preceded.
Next, invite [the deities] of the central court according to the previous method.
Next, invite [the deities] of the outer court, also according to the previous method.
In this manner, one should summon all the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas of the Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣavijaya, the various Bodhisattvas, the Vajra-Bodhisattvas, the celestial deities, and so forth,
while sequentially binding their respective root mudrās.
If one invites the Buddha, one should form the aforementioned seal for inviting the Buddha.
If one invites the Bodhisattva One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣacakravartin and other Uṣṇīṣacakravartin Bodhisattvas, one should form the seal for collectively summoning all Uṣṇīṣacakravartins.
If one invites all Bodhisattvas, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas, [one should likewise form the appropriate seal].
All should form the *vajra-samādhi-vīrya-mudrā* of all Tathāgatas.
Their welcoming mudrās and sitting mudrās are to be performed according to the preceding mudrās.
The inner court, middle court, and outer court shall all follow their designated positions in the painting.
Recite the names of each Buddha, the names of each Bodhisattva, the names of each Vajra-holder, and the names of the various devas.
While forming mudrās and reciting mantras, invoke them by name with prostrations.
In this manner, having individually invited the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and various celestial deities,
and having visualized each as they were invited,
the general invitation for all to take their respective positions within the ritual mandala is completed.
To perform the seal for binding the boundary with the command of the Great Samādhi,
follow the previous seal for inviting the Buddhas,
but modify it by placing each index finger over the upper joint of its respective middle finger.
Bend both thumbs so that they rest against the lower joints of the index fingers.
With the palms of the two hands four inches apart,
place the mudrā upon the crown of the head and, with reverence, slowly rotate it three times to the right, following the path of the sun.
Recite the heart-mantra of Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣavijaya.
Recite the four syllables *bandha bandha* seven times,
and then issue this command:
Having established the boundary through samādhi and being fully endowed with dignified deportment,
he invited the assembly of noble ones to take their positions according to the Dharma and sit upon their seats.
Furthermore, at the western gate, he joined his palms, prostrated, and knelt respectfully.
Holding an incense burner, burn various famous incenses and visualize all the painted Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and all celestial deities,
each seated upon their respective thrones as their true reward bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Moving his gaze, he beheld the Buddha manifesting the appearance of preaching the Dharma.
He then addressed the Buddha with these words, requesting that the boundary be established:

"I pray that all the assembly of noble ones will each occupy their respective seats, maintaining full dignified deportment and dwelling in accordance with the Dharma. Having spoken these words, he immediately took a silver platter and various powdered incenses.
Cupping the incense with both hands, recite the Heart Mantra of Sarvavajradhātviśvarī seven times over the powdered incense,
and scatter it from within the inner court upon Tathāgata Śākyamuni and upon the various Bodhisattvas of the five Vajradhātviśvarīs.
Next, one should scatter [the offerings] everywhere over all the Buddhas in the third enclosure,
as well as over all the Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and so forth,
continuing until they are scattered entirely over all the celestial deities and others, making universal offerings to them all.

Again, take a silver platter containing flowers, cup them with both hands, and recite the mantra seven times; then, as in the ritual for scattering incense, offer them universally. This is called the offering of the Samādhi Dhāraṇī of Incense.
Perform the offering with the Mantra of the Samādhi of the Named Flower.
Having performed this rite,
again take hold of the vajra with the left hand.
Holding a rosary in his right hand, he says:
"I, [Name], now revere and uphold all the infinite treasuries of the Prajñāpāramitā and its myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Now, from all the Buddhas of the ten directions,
I reverently receive this Dharma.
Having spoken these words, he immediately raised both hands, placing them upon his head in reverent veneration.
Performing the ritual in this manner is called the method for receiving and upholding [the teaching] with head-shouldering and reverence.
Furthermore, place the rosary, vajra, and other implements upon a silver platter and prostrate to the World-Honored One.
Holding an incense burner in his hand, he burned incense as an offering,
circumambulated the altar three times, took leave of the Buddha, and withdrew.
He then entered the third inner court and the second outer court.

With various kinds of incense, flowers, ghee, honey, curd, granulated sugar, milk porridge, yogurt porridge, sesame porridge, rice, cakes, and fruits—such foods and fruits as these were all fresh and excellent.
Using plates made of gold, silver, copper, and so forth,
arrange and present them according to the ritual rules, placing each one in its proper position on the four sides.
Furthermore, offer ghee, honey, milk, curd, milk-gruel, curd-gruel, various fragrant flowers, all kinds of food and drink, as well as fruits and other such items.
In the outer courtyard, they arranged themselves in rows on all four sides to make offerings.
