In the inner courtyard, wax candles were lit at each of the four corners and along the four sides;
lamps were also lit around the outer courtyard as offerings, arranged to form a garland of light.
Furthermore, take small portions of all food, drink, flowers, and fruits,
and place them as if in a vessel filled with pure water. Then,
carry them to a location beneath a pure tree or within a grove of bamboo.
Recite the mantra three times, calling upon all ghosts and spirits to come and partake of my ambrosial food and drink.
Upon casting it upon the ground, they will immediately turn back and depart.
By performing this rite of giving, one’s blessings and fortune will increase.
This is the extensive ritual for this maṇḍala, covering the various procedures and methods for constructing the altar from the first day until the final day,
as well as the methods for the ācārya.
The method for instructing disciples,
the method for entering the maṇḍala,
and the method for conferring empowerment are all to be applied according to the various Great Empowerment Sūtras and the rules for maṇḍala rituals.
The wise should know that those who perform this rite, along with their companions and close disciples,
must all enter and exit together after bathing for purification;
they should adorn the mandala and refrain from idle speech or laughter.
Single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.
Each person should have three pairs of robes, all of which must be new and clean;
one pair is for entering the ritual platform.
One pair shall partake of food;
another pair shall go outside for walking meditation and using the toilet.
The ācārya shall then enter the maṇḍala once again.
He circumambulated the inner and outer courtyards to the right, walking along the path and observing them all around.
He considered which of the various articles of adornment were in accordance with the Dharma and which were not,
and he commanded his disciples to restore the adornments accordingly.
Having adorned oneself,
exit the maṇḍala and wash the hands and rinse the mouth according to the ritual rules.
Then, as before, form the Great Samaya Seal of the Command of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.
Recite the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.
After each repetition, add the four syllables *bandha bandha*.
Seal the four directions, the four corners, and the center in the air with the mudrā.
Circumambulate three times to the right, ensuring the sound of the mantra does not cease.
Having completed four circumambulations in the intermediate directions, one should again address [the deity], saying:
"The King of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa has fully perfected the majestic deportment of the samādhi boundary."
One should address the assembly of noble ones, requesting them to abide according to the Dharma and accept the various offerings;
then, once the proceedings are complete, one performs this ritual procedure,
which is called the "Great Boundary-Establishment" (Mahā-sīmā-bandha).
He settles himself in meditative composure.
Furthermore, the practitioner again goes to the western gate,
joins his palms in prostration, circumambulates the altar, and performs the ritual walk.
Perform prostrations at each gate and offer praise in Sanskrit.
Visualize that this maṇḍala is adorned with all manner of splendors,
like the assembly where the Buddha preached the Dharma at the Bodhi tree in the Vajra-maṇḍala.
One should conceive a sense of wonder,
visualizing the principal deity, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial deities, mantra-deities, mantra-sages, and nāga-kings, each one in succession as being identical to their true bodies.
Furthermore, at the western gate of the fourth courtyard, kneel lengthwise and form the mudrā.
Recite the mantra seven times over the incense burner while maintaining the mudrā;
then, holding the incense burner, burn various kinds of famous incense.
Recite this mantra universally for all devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings; for kings, royal lineages, ministers, and officials;

for all teachers, monks, parents, and donors of the ten directions throughout past and present lives; and for all sentient beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth, as well as fellow practitioners.
Furthermore, each person should burn one pellet of incense for themselves.
With focused visualization, they should imagine clouds of incense, food, drink,
and all manner of flowers and fruits to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Pañcaśīrṣacakravartin,
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
and the Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddhi.
The Bodhisattva Cakravartī-vināśana,
the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā,
and the Bodhisattva Samantavyūha-cakravartī.
The Bodhisattva Tathāgata-Ūrṇā-lakṣaṇa,
up to the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-daṃṣṭra,
and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva,
as well as all the Buddhas, all the Bodhisattvas, all the Vajras, and all the celestial sages of the outer enclosure, together with their respective retinues,
were all seated in their original positions as if before one's eyes.
Before each [deity], one should make offerings according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, one should direct the mind to visualize these clouds of incense pervading all Buddha-fields and various Dharma assemblies at the bodhimandas throughout the ten directions.
Each and every one makes offerings to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and all celestial immortals.
Such clouds of incense, within each and every Buddha-field,
transform into fragrant palaces, halls, and pavilions.
Pavilions and ponds made of the seven treasures,
subtle and wondrous sounds,
and ocean-like clouds of offerings for all Buddha-activities.
Cloud-oceans of offerings consisting of all kinds of precious flowers—mandārava flowers, māndāravas, kumuda flowers, and campaka flowers;
and cloud-oceans of offerings consisting of all kinds of powdered incense.
Ocean-clouds of offerings of all kinds of unguents;
ocean-clouds of offerings of all kinds of incenses;
ocean-clouds of offerings of all kinds of extraordinary and magnificent great maṇi jewels.
Ocean-like clouds of offerings consisting of various kinds of ambrosial food and drink from all the devas;
ocean-like clouds of offerings consisting of various kinds of wondrous garments and necklaces from all the devas.
Oceans of clouds of offerings consisting of all the most exquisite celestial flower garlands, jeweled crowns, rings,
and bracelets fill the entire dharma-realm and all buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, making offerings to them.

Furthermore, throughout the ten directions, reaching all beings of the six realms and four modes of birth who suffer from illness and affliction, as well as all sentient beings undergoing suffering in the various hells,
it emits a harmonious and elegant sound, extolling the Triple Gem.
Upon hearing this and attaining it accordingly, one is freed from the various painful sensations of the hells.
It fulfills the wishes of sentient beings;
for those afflicted by illness, the fragrant clouds enter their bodies.
It removes all physical and mental ailments and afflictions.
One should likewise constantly perform such offerings during all mantra recitations.
Prostrate to all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas.
Circumambulating the altar while walking the path, they join their palms in praise and admiration.
Having made great and expansive vows, they take leave of the Buddha and exit the altar grounds.
Those who have received the Dharma possess refined and handsome faculties, and their natures are pure and upright as they resolve upon the mind of Bodhi.
Having bathed in fragrant water and donned fresh, clean robes, one should, according to the Dharma,
openly confess and repent for all transgressions of the present actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds.
Having conferred the three refuges, he asks:

To deliver sentient beings, one must endure manifold sufferings while dwelling alone in mountain valleys, all for the sake of fame and profit.
If one recites with this thought, yet lacks realization and fails to achieve accomplishment,
the Buddha censures these three types of practitioners. Therefore, one should turn the mind toward the Dharma and for the sake of sentient beings, abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
In this world there are three types of non-Buddhist minds: Some deny everything as being of self-nature;
Some preach that cause and effect do not exist; Some claim that nothing is attained through cultivation.
How can these be called the King of Mantras? Only by practicing until one reaches the stage of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) Is one truly a master of mantras.
Therefore, one should contemplate these two dharmas: diligence and merit share the same cause.
They subdue all classes of celestial beings and immortals. A wise person should not slander those who lack wisdom and possess faults;
for even a practitioner who has achieved little may appear as though they have attained much.
Those who recite mantras and claim to be true knowers, yet do not become Buddhas for the benefit of the world—
such is the dharma of the wheel-turning kings (cakravartin). They perform sacrifices to all the gods according to the three clans,
yet they do not take refuge or pay homage [to the Buddha].
Such are the dharmas of the Wheel-Turning King;
the sequential rites have been taught as above. May all practitioners uphold them.
*The Scripture of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin*, Scroll Four.
The Scripture of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin, Scroll Five, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: The Accomplishment of the World. Chapter Ten: The Accomplishment of the World.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata again entered the samādhi of the miraculous manifestation of the realm of the King of the Light of the Dharma, the Pinnacle of All Buddhas' Inconceivable Dhāraṇīs.

At that very time, all those Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges also entered the samādhi of the miraculous manifestation of the realm of the King of the Light of the Dharma at the Pinnacle of the Inconceivable Dhāraṇī of All Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secret Traces,
rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence,
circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.
They gazed upon the Tathāgata with unblinking eyes.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni,
together with all the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [appeared].
Rising serenely from samādhi,
he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
"Listen attentively and quietly to the Five-Crested Wheel-King of all Buddhas."
Diverse mantras share the same dharma;
they can accomplish the immeasurable majestic power and immeasurable karmic activities of the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin-mantra, the Buddhalocanā-mantra,
and others, and can manifest various kinds of great inconceivabilities.
To benefit sentient beings,
from within a single seal (*mudrā*) arise differentiated seals;
these differentiated seals are employed universally.
Because these all accomplish immeasurable deeds.
Regarding the first of the root heart-seals of the Sarvatathāgata-uṣṇīṣa-rāja: with the two left index fingers, the two ring fingers, and the two little fingers.
Interlace the right hand over the left, inserting them into the palms to form fists.
Then, bend both thumbs double and insert their tips into the palms.
Finally, extend the two middle fingers straight upward with their tips joined together.
This is the Single Dharma Seal, a rite for achieving the crowns of all Buddhas.
It subjugates all evil devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and vināyakas.
Upon seeing this mudrā, all [demons] flee in terror. The mantra for this mudrā is:
*Namaḥ vāgīśvarāya viśvasenāya oṃ hūṃ jvala hūṃ bandha svāhā*. This single mudrā and mantra possess great majestic power (*mahā-tejas*).
If one constantly binds the wheel to protect oneself and others,
one will attain great peace and happiness, eliminate all suffering,
and benefit all sentient beings.
It can also accomplish all ritual activities.
Regarding the two mudrās for summoning the Universal Sovereign (Sarvatathāgata-uṣṇīṣa-rāja), they correspond to the root mudrā.
Using only the tips of the two middle fingers, move them slightly up and down. The mudrā and mantra are as follows:

*Namo bhagavate viśvasya ehy ehi bhagavan dharmanirghoṣa mama [insert name here] kṣipraṃ jñāpayasva.* *Na-mo bha-ga-ba-te bi-shwa-sya e-hi e-hi bha-ga-ban da-rma-nir-gho-sha ma-ma [name] kship-raṃ jy-na-pa-ya-swa.* (The mantra concludes with the word *jñāpayasva*, meaning "make known" or "reveal," followed by the practitioner's own name.)
*Śabdāpaya balindramocaka paritrāyasva vārapāra kṣaramaya svāhā.* This is the mantra of the mudrā.

Holding white flowers, recite the mantra three times to invite all Buddhas and the assembly of the Bodhisattvas of the Five-Crested Wheel-King (*Pañcakula-cakravartin*) to take their seats within the maṇḍala.
[Recite] the three seals and mantras for the offerings to all Wheel-Kings; regarding these, the offering seals are to be employed according to the standard offering seals used elsewhere.
Namo bhagavate viśvasya om vajra-krodha-bhṛkuṭī-vidrāvaṇa-vajriṇi phaṭ phaṭ vaḍini phaṭ cara cara raṭi ccha gara gara sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite dharmarāja īśvara-adhipate svāhā. This is the Dharma-mantra.
When making offerings, hold aloft unguents, incense, scented water, flowers, and various foods and drinks;
recite the mantra three times over each and present them as an offering.
All four seals for summoning the Fire Deity of the Sarvatathāgata-uṣṇīṣa-śīrṣa follow the root seal.
Only change the two middle fingers,
bending them into the shape of a half-ring;
their tips must not touch one another.
This is the single Dharma-seal.
One should invite the Fire God (Agni) and make offerings to him;
once the offerings have been presented, one should then dismiss the Fire God.
Then, with the hands drawn back and straightened, extend the tips of the two middle fingers. The mantra is:
*Namo bhagavate viśvasya ehe ehi tiṣṭha maṇḍe ṛkṣanade svāhā*. When burning fire offerings (*homāhāra*), recite this seal-mantra three times.
First, invite the Fire Deity (Agnideva) to consume the offerings.
Only after that should one offer the food to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and all the mantra-deities.
Regarding the five seal-mantras for dispatching the Fire Deity of the Sarvatathāgata-uṣṇīṣa-rāja: these dispatch seals are to be employed according to the previously mentioned invitation seals.

*Namo bhagavate viśvasya jaye jaya tiṣṭha mā riṣe rakṣaṇāye svāhā.* Having completed the offering of the fire-oblation with this single-seal mantra, recite it twenty-one times and dismiss the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*).
The Sixth: Invoking the Mudrās and Mantras of the Five Uṣṇīṣa Kings. These mudrās and mantras for invocation are to be used according to the previous [section on] the invocation mudrās.

*Namo bhagavate uṣṇīṣāya oṃ hūṃ jvālārte oṃ hūṃ jvala-arte oṃ hūṃ māmaka hūṃ māraṇi svāhā oṃ hūṃ mama mama hūṃ māraṇi.* This single mudrā and mantra invoke the Five Uṣṇīṣa Kings, as well as all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, mantra-siddhas, and deities.
It is also applicable for the ritual applications of offering unguents, scattering flowers, and burning incense.
Regarding the seventh seal of the Cakravartin King Crusher, it follows the fundamental seal.
Simply bend the tip of the right middle finger and rest it upon the first joint of the left middle finger;
keep the left middle finger straight and upright.
This single Dharma-seal is also called the Seal for Purifying the Ground;
it possesses the power to accomplish all matters, including the binding of boundaries,
protection of the body, purification of the ground, and consecration.
The seal and mantra to be used for all [these cases] are as follows:
*Namo bhagavate viśvasya oṃ hūṃ mīgilāna duna duna du*. If one is afflicted by obstacles caused by Vināyakas, this single seal and mantra should be employed.
One should always use this mantra for consecrating by sprinkling water (*abhiṣeka*), protecting the body, establishing the boundary (*sīmābandha*), and binding the ritual altar (*maṇḍala*);
it is universally applicable for all such purposes.

If one is constructing the great dharma-altar of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King, when purifying the dwelling, one should recite this mantra over fire, food, ashes, white mustard seeds, and other substances.
Recite one hundred and eight times in unison;
scatter [the water] throughout the four directions inside and outside the dwelling to purify the boundaries.
Alternatively, one may consecrate water, ashes, and so forth with the heart-mantra of the Sarvavid Vairocana King of All Crowns and sprinkle them everywhere;
or one may consecrate them using the body-mantra or heart-mantra that one habitually recites and maintains.

Furthermore, recite the mantra of the Cakravartin King of Destruction one hundred and eight times over four stakes made of khadira wood and drive them into the four directions to demarcate the boundary of the maṇḍala.
The Eighth Seal of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King for Subduing All Evil Deities and Ghosts: Following the Root Seal.
Simply bend the tip of the left middle finger and rest it upon the first joint of the right middle finger;
keep the right middle finger straight and upright.
This is the Seal of the Single Dharma;
it is also called the Heart-Seal of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.
Its power is able to subdue obstructing Vināyakas and all malevolent spirits and ghosts; one should constantly employ this seal.
This subdues all obstacles and difficulties.
It may be universally applied for consecration and ritual bathing to eliminate all hindrances and afflictions.
The seal and mantra are as follows: *Namo bhagavate viśvasya sarvamitrāṇāṃ prabhūtotsāhāya svāhā.* This is the Dharma-mantra.
It can subdue all malevolent spirits and ghosts,
and by means of incantations, protect and shield one's companions and body.
Standing firm in the four directions, it performs the Great Dharma.
The Ninth Seal of the Great Mahāduṣprasaha-krodharāja:
Following the root seal, simply modify it by bending the two middle fingers.
The right hand presses down upon the left;
each thumb stands upright, pressing against the backs of the fingers on both sides at their joints.
This is a single *mudrā*.
If one constantly ties this wheel-knot,
it can extinguish all sins and bring about great peace and security; furthermore,
one shall not have evil dreams.
For the *śāntika* rite, this is specifically employed as the supreme seal-mantra.
It is as follows: *Namo bhagavate śāntisvarasvāmine sarvatathāgatādhipataye | Oṃ hūṃ śamaya śamaya śāntiṃ kuru dharma-rāja vaśī mahābuddhi-sarva-ḍākinī svāhā.* This is the single seal-mantra.
Take a brand-new, clean two-dou measure white earthenware jar,
fill it completely with scented water,
and place it at the center of the altar.
If one recites the mantra one thousand and eight times and performs an ablution for consecration,
it can dispel all defilements of sin, calamities, and obstacles caused by vināyakas;
one shall obtain peace day and night, and all evil dreams shall be eliminated.
Guhya-pati, this is a brief explanation of a single seal.
From it, various seals arise according to the applications of the dharmas.
If one were to explain them extensively, there would be such widespread incantations and instructions for practice.
Each and every dharma has an immeasurable and extensive explanation that is not merely provisional.

Why is this? Because I have already extensively analyzed, in other sections, the methods for the Five-Crested Wheel-Turning King Mantras together with the Buddhalocanā Mantra and various other mantras.
Therefore, herein I shall briefly explain the mantra methods for the accomplishment of the Five-Crested Wheel-Turning King (Pañcamudrācakravartin).
Through the supernatural power of these mantras, one realizes liberation.
This was spoken by the sons of all Buddhas.
It is said that by the power of diligence, one vows to benefit sentient beings from their various sufferings and cause them to receive worldly peace and happiness;
thus, it is known that the reciter of the mantra acts for the benefit of sentient beings by severing the net of all doubts.
If one practices with the exertion of diligent effort, one will realize accomplishment. Guhyapati,
if a practitioner of mantras should fail to achieve realization despite long-term upholding of the mantra with great diligence, [it is due to a lack of such effort].
Furthermore, one should construct a square altar measuring four cubits on each side.
Having plastered the site of the altar according to the ritual rules,
one should paint a single-cubit lotus flower with one hundred and eight petals made of the seven precious gems at its center.
Upon the flower pedestal, draw a wheel of seven jewels.
Furthermore, at the eastern gate, draw the seal of a multicolored wheel;
next, at the southern gate, draw the seal of a three-pronged trident in various colors.
Next, at the head of the western gate, paint a multicolored nāga-king seal.
Next, at the head of the northern gate, paint a multicolored three-pronged vajra.
Next, draw a cross within each of the four corners.
Second, the mudrā of the five-pronged golden vajra:
fill two clean, white porcelain jars with scented water and place them upright at the center of the mandala upon the lotus pedestal.
Every day, apply the mantra of the Great Difficult-to-Conquer Furenu (Krodharāja) King;
recite it one thousand and eight times according to the ritual rules for self-protection, and again seven times.
Perform the consecration bath and make vows with body, speech, and mind.
Recite the vow as in the previously described Great Empowerment Ritual, and so forth.
Perform this three times daily for twenty-one days or forty-nine days,
reciting according to the previous method.
Immediately, all obstacles, vināyakas, malevolent stars, calamities, and portents shall be entirely dispersed and subdued;
merit and virtue will increase, and one will swiftly realize the Great Samādhi of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King Mantra.
The Lord of Secret Traces is the Five-Crested Wheel-King.
Furthermore, there is a minor rite:
simply by recollecting, chanting, and maintaining it while forming the Tathāgata-Uṣṇīṣa Mudrā.
Seal it upon the crown of the head with the mantra-seal three times,
and protection will be established.
Alternatively, one may use the ashes of burnt food offerings.
Alternatively, one may recite the mantra over white mustard seeds seven times;
by wearing them on the head, the topknot, or the body, one will likewise achieve protection.
Should there be any calamities, malevolent spirits, or various illnesses, [they shall be averted].
Tie white thread with one knot for each mantra;
by wearing it upon the body or neck, [all obstacles] shall be eliminated.
This applies when performing various rites in a cemetery (śmaśāna).
Forming the mudrā and reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times will protect and benefit the body,
allowing one to perform whatever rites as desired.
For *śāntika* rites, follow the procedures set forth below.
If one recites the mantra once over each portion of clarified butter and burns it, the rite will be accomplished.
If one wishes to retrieve hidden treasures,
they should be purified by smelting.
Recite the mantra once and burn one portion of ghee, repeating this one thousand and eight times;
thus one will obtain freedom from obstacles.
Alternatively, by reciting the mantra once and burning one white mustard seed, repeating this one thousand and eight times, one likewise attains freedom from obstacles.
If one wishes to open the gate of the asuras,
one should first touch the随心坛 (suixintan) [the altar according to one's mind],

burn incense, and perform offerings while reciting three lakṣas— where "one lakṣa" in the Sanskrit language means a number of one hundred thousand in Chinese— until the bolts and keys of the asura gate break and open.
Furthermore, take white mustard seeds and salt in equal portions and mix them with one's own *rūdraka* berries.
At each of the three times of day, hold two fingers' worth between the thumb and forefinger;
recite the mantra once for each pinch and burn it one thousand and eight times.
When the twenty-first day has passed, great fires shall break out in all the cave-palaces of the asuras.
The hosts of asura women will emerge from the cave gates together to welcome the incantation-master and bestow upon him the medicine of longevity.
The siddhis of the pestle, wheel, sword,
and realgar; or again, having respectfully invited [the deity] into the cave,
if the practitioner sees a malevolent asura, [he should act].
One should form the Tathāgatoṣṇīṣa mudrā.
Reciting the mantra once while casting the seal forward,
if this is done seven times, [the opponent] will fall to the ground in a swoon.
Furthermore, there is a method: always consume a gruel made of barley milk.
Recite the mantra one million three hundred thousand times (three lakṣas).
Then, upon awakening from a dream, [the goal will be attained].
One obtains the elixir of longevity and consumes it.
Furthermore, there is a method for performing this during a lunar eclipse:
one should rub the altar and burn incense.
At that time, the mantra-reciter must especially not look at the moon.
Place silver vessels filled with milk at the center of the altar;
by reciting the mantra with single-minded concentration over the milk, the moon will return to its former state.
If one drinks it immediately, it can eliminate all calamities within the body.
Furthermore, there is a method: go to a mountain peak and dwell there, constantly eating rice and milk porridge.
Facing east, sit cross-legged.
Form the mudrā and recite the mantra for three hundred thousand times (*tri-lakṣa*).
Then, for three days and three nights, abstain from food and speech.
Having cut wood from the Bodhi tree to kindle a fire, one should take equal portions of these—sesame, ghee, and curd—and mix them together.
For three days and three nights, one should recite the mantra once for each offering, burning them without interruption.
When three days and nights have passed and the dawn is about to break,
one will naturally obtain auspicious wealth and treasures.
Furthermore, one should construct a *cittamaṇḍala* (mind-pleasing altar) on the summit of the mountain.
Place the śarīra-stūpa precisely at the center of the altar.
Always sit cross-legged facing east before the stūpa.
Recite the mantra over a lotus flower once every day.
If one places [the beads] before a stūpa until they reach one lakṣa,
those who have short lifespans and meager merit will see their fortune and longevity doubled.
Furthermore, there is a method:
go to a riverbank and smear pure white sandalwood paste upon lotus flowers.
Recite the mantra once for each flower and cast them into the river until one *lakṣa* has been completed.
It shall also cleanse away karmic defilements, and one’s merit and auspiciousness will increase ever further.
Furthermore, there is a method wherein white mustard seeds are mixed with oil;
at each of the three periods of the day, one should recite the mantra once and burn [the mixture] once.
Recite it one thousand and eight times.
When seven days have passed, others will come to respect and submit to you of their own accord.
Furthermore, there is another method: if you wish for pure-practicing brahmins to respectfully praise and submit to you.
When burning white flowers,
if one wishes to gain the respect, affection, and submission of kṣatriyas,
one should burn yellow flowers.
If one wishes for those who cultivate fields to love, revere, and submit to one in accordance with the Dharma,
one should burn black flowers.
If one wishes to cause heterodox views and evil persons to be subdued and brought under control, [one should likewise perform this rite].
Take equal parts of rice husks, leaves of the *karañja* tree, and poison;
mix them together and incense them one by one while reciting the mantra once for each.
Thus, one will achieve the power of invisibility.
If one punishes an enemy,
by chanting the mantra once for each black mustard seed and burning them,
that person will be subdued. If one wishes to subdue bhūtas and piśācas, [one should proceed in the same manner].
Burn one piece of saffron for each recitation, performing this separately one thousand and eight times.
When three days and nights have passed, [the spirit] will naturally submit out of respect. If you wish to dispatch it to subjugate a disease-demon, [perform the rite accordingly].
Form the mudrā and recite the mantra;
at the end of each repetition of the mantra,
further add the recitation of the syllable *phaṭ*.
If a person is afflicted by insect venom or medicinal poison,
resulting in distress and pain,
the mantra-reciter shall recite the mantra over them; with each complete recitation, they shall be restored.
Furthermore, recite the two characters *jo ning* seven times;
again, add the three characters *mo mo mo* seven times;
and again, add the character *ji* seven times.
Furthermore, add the two characters "jiān-mù" seven times.
Reciting these added characters silently in this manner will restrain and subdue poisons.
If one wishes to restrain ghosts, [the same applies].
In the mantra, further add the syllables *ṭiṣṭha ṭiṣṭha*.

Alternatively, one may add *kaca* (pronounced with the retroflex *c* as in *ku-juna*), or *kṣa* (pronounced with the sibilant *kṣ* as in *shu-jia*). By adding *kṣa*, the body is restrained and held still.
If one adds the character *ḍa* (pronounced with a rolled tongue;
the same applies below for *ḍa-ḍa*), it will restrain the ghosts so that their throat-gas cannot pass or be released.
Furthermore, another method is to take one hundred and eight peacock feathers.
Bind them together in one place.
During a solar or lunar eclipse, rub the altar and install the image.
One should place a peacock’s tail in front of the image.
Forming mudrās and reciting mantras, one consecrates the peacock tail;
then, one waits until the sun and moon have returned to their normal state.
Holding this tail, one uses it accordingly to shake and sweep.
It can bring about all auspicious dharmas.
If one brushes against a person afflicted by poison, the poison will gradually be eliminated.
All such practices, when cultivated according to their respective instructions, will be fully accomplished.
If one wishes to [exorcise] calamities, punishments, ghosts, spirits, or illnesses,
one should mix salt with oil and burn it while reciting the mantra once for each portion;
thus, the calamities, ghosts, and illnesses will be dispelled.
Furthermore, there is another method: fashion an image of a ghost using cow dung.
Place it before the [deity's] image and hold a blade.
With each recitation of the mantra, cut off a hand, a foot, or a limb and joint of the ghost's form.
This can cause true spirits to suffer pain in their limbs and joints.
If one desires abundance,
one should kindle a fire using various types of milky wood, cutting them all at once.
Take various fruits and grains mixed with clarified butter and honey;
recite the mantra once for each offering and burn them, and then one's wishes will be fulfilled as desired.
Furthermore, there is another method: mix white sesame seeds with clarified butter and honey.
Chanting the mantra once and burning [the substance] once will likewise fulfill one's wishes.

Furthermore, there is another method: cut *kuruṇṭaka* grass into inch-long pieces, mix them with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and chant the mantra once while burning each piece until one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) have been completed.
Thus, one transforms right action so that merit and lifespan exceed [ordinary] longevity.
Furthermore, there is a method wherein by reciting a mantra once over clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and burning it once, one attains great majestic power (*mahā-tejas*).
Moreover, there is a method wherein by mixing clarified butter and milk together and reciting a mantra once over them and burning them once, one attains great peace and stability (*mahā-śānti*).
Furthermore, there is a method: by mixing clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and curd (*dadhi*) together, reciting the mantra once for each oblation, one obtains great wealth and food.
In this manner, one should offer the fire-oblations three times daily, performing one thousand and eight repetitions for each session.
Upon the completion of seven days for each, one attains accomplishment.
Furthermore, O Lord of Secret Traces (Guhyakādhipati),
there is also the Great Dharma King of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakra-Rāja, which brings about the accomplishment of the Great Dharma Joy.
At a site containing relics or on the summit of a high mountain,
burn incense as an offering and sit cross-legged facing east.
Form the mudrā and recite the mantra for three hundred thousand times (*tri-lakṣa*).
Then, having fried rice chaff and mixed it with ghee, curd, and honey,
one should sit cross-legged before the image and consume three finger-measures of it at each of the three times of the day.
Recite the mantra once for each incense offering, repeating this one thousand and eight times until a total of one lakṣa has been reached;
then proceed to a mountain where there are pine and cypress forests.
For three days and three nights, he did not eat nor speak;
facing east, he sat in the lotus posture with the corners of his *kāṣāya* robe tied together.
Recite the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King until it reaches one lakṣa. If one is a layperson,
recite the mantra over one's hair while combing and tying it until it reaches one lakṣa.
One immediately realizes the *ādhāraṇa* [meditative concentration];
while wandering through the world, one is not seen by others.
Furthermore, according to the method, one should go to a mountain peak and dwell there.
At every meal, he consumed barley milk gruel;
he constantly faced the sun in the full lotus posture and recited the mantra for one *lakṣa*.
One will also attain the realization of *āntardhāna*.
Furthermore, there is a method: form a fist with the left hand and recite the mantra for one *lakṣa*; one will realize the aforementioned dharma.
Furthermore, according to another method, when there is a lunar eclipse,
one should smear the随心坛 (Sui-xin-tan) with [sandalwood paste] and place a red copper vessel filled with red-yellow cow’s ghee inside the altar.
Using red copper tongs, stir the clarified butter continuously while reciting the mantra until three signs appear:
first, the sign of froth.
If the person reciting the mantra consumes it, they will attain great dhāraṇī power.
Second, the manifestation of the sign of smoke;
the practitioner who consumes it attains great *ānantarya*.
Third, the manifestation of the sign of light.
One who ingests this mantra-elixir will attain the supernormal knowledge of consciousness and be able to know the three periods of time.
The method for accomplishing the realgar rite is likewise.
Furthermore, there are the sites of reliquary stupas,
the summits of high mountains,
and forest hermitages (āraṇya).
In deep mountain valleys,
by rivers, springs, and ponds,
one should practice the rites of the wheel, the sword, the vajra, the staff, and the black antelope skin.
Each person shall first recite the mantra one thousand and eight times;
thereafter, they shall perform the ritual according to the dharma and recite the mantra.
This is because they shall all realize the samaya of the three kinds of siddhi mentioned above.
Furthermore, there is another method: using unhusked rice and *taṇḍula*,
one should bathe thoroughly, put on fresh clean garments,
place a flower garland upon the head, and smear an eight-cubit altar.
At the center of the altar, lie facing upward with your head toward the east; this is Maitreya.
Furthermore, take four stakes made of khadira wood.
Drive them deep into the ground,
then bind the two hands and two feet of Mitraka to the four stakes.
The practitioner of the mantra shall likewise bathe thoroughly, protect the body, and establish the boundary.
Eat the three white foods.
Mount upon this *maitrāyaṇī* (rice-bag).
First, recite the mantra over the *maitrāyaṇī* thirty-one thousand and eight times.
One should then take milk porridge;

Chapter Twelve: On the Realization of the Dharma. From the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin-sūtra*, Chapter Twelve: On the Realization of the Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One perceived that all sentient beings within the realm of phenomena were entangled by the thick covering of ignorance, defiled by obscurations, and their [minds] remained fragmented and unextinguished.
He further addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"For the sake of all bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen,
and laywomen who wish to achieve mastery in this inconceivable one-syllable Cakravartin King Seal-Mantra, I [shall teach it]."
This explains the gateway of the samaya to be practiced:
one should each maintain pure precepts, resolve upon bodhicitta,
and request the ācārya.
Having performed the consecration of the dharma-maṇḍala for receiving the teachings,
one’s conduct shall be purified according to the Dharma and one’s roots of goodness shall be fully perfected.
Relying upon a spiritual friend, one should practice the recollection of the six mindfulnesses.
Through skillful means, they contemplate and realize that suchness, the true dharma, and the dharmadhātu are of the nature of space;
they enter into profound prajñāpāramitā with a mind free from duality and non-dual conduct, remaining ever heedful.
One does not engage in false speech.
One is never abrupt or violent.
Nor does one mock or provoke others out of anger, affliction, or pride.
They slander sentient beings; yet,
relying on the practice of the Dharma within the realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time,
they skillfully understand, discern, rejoice in, and cultivate it.
Disregarding one's own body and life, one should leave the human world and dwell in an araṇya,
generating the bodhicitta three times each day and taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
One should formally vow to receive the bodhisattva precepts according to the Dharma,
retain them in memory without forgetting as they have been heard and studied,
contemplate the meaning of the teachings, and cultivate the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
They sweep and clean the Buddha-stūpas and maṇḍalas as an offering;
they arouse a mind of diligent vigor with body and speech focused on a single purpose;
and they abide in inner and outer purity within the mark of non-abiding.
One should always be humble, respectful, and harmonious toward one’s preceptors, instructors, and fellow students;
one should have compassion for sentient beings and thoroughly comprehend the profound Dharma gates of esoteric meaning;
and one should constantly delight in diligence to deliver and liberate sentient beings.
Abiding in the Buddha-way,
through such correspondence, one shall attain the realization of the Dharma of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin King;
in a future life, one’s body will be the color of pure gold.
His marks and signs were exceptionally sublime and possessed inconceivable qualities.
He was adorned purely with earrings, bracelets, flower crowns, and necklaces made of the seven precious gems.
The radiance of his physical form surpassed that of a hundred thousand suns.
It eclipsed all other forms so that none appeared.
Secret Lord, having thus accomplished the rite of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King,
all those who saw him were filled with great joy.
Just as the wish-fulfilling tree fulfills all that is desired,
furthermore, Guhyapati, if there is a bodhisattva who realizes this Dharma of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King of Uṣṇīṣas.
If one joyfully offers the various exquisite foods of the Nirmāṇarati devas as rain to all sentient beings in the hells,
they will all be fully satisfied.
One shall also attain the fulfillment of worldly aspirations and joys.
If there are those who resolve their minds for the sake of all sentient beings and practice the rite of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King, they shall achieve success.
"Even Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages cannot obstruct this Dharma of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King.
Guhyapati, this mantra is the most supreme among all mantras."
If one achieves this, the ten thousand practices of a bodhisattva will all be perfected;
all ten grave transgressions and their defilements,

Having attained the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they travel throughout the Akaniṣṭha Heaven in a single kṣaṇa;
practicing the bodhisattva conduct, they become objects of joy for all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and devas, and receive their praise.
If one wishes to travel to all infinite and boundless worlds to guide and transform sentient beings,
teaching the various dharmas in accordance with their respective languages and sounds;
They also travel to immeasurable and boundless varieties of worlds,
manifesting various bodies according to each world,
all of which are exquisitely beautiful.
According to their respective forms and types, his speech was without exception entirely perfect and complete.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
"The person who accomplishes the Dharma of the Cakravartin King of Uṣṇīṣas, In physical marks and signs surpasses even the Tārās and gods."
The various mantra-seers and gods of great majesty, each holding a sword or a blue lotus, clash and swirl like shifting clouds;

Guhya-pati, I shall now further briefly explain for all mantra-practitioners three types of places for the accomplishment of the stages (*bhūmi-siddhi-sthāna*).
The first is the superior stage (*uttama-bhūmi*).
Second is the middle realm;
third is the lower realm;
these are the pure and impure places.
Thus, each of these three stages further contains three;
the wise understand this well.
As for what is called the "higher stage":
It is said that there are three supreme grounds in the heavens through which one achieves the highest *siddhi*.
As for what is called the middle ground:
That is to say, in the valleys of great rivers, the shores of the ocean, and within mountains;
in these three places, middling *siddhi* is accomplished.
As for what is called the "lower ground":
That is to say: at great springs and ponds where lotuses grow;
in groves of many flowers and fruits;
and in śmaśāna charnel grounds.
In this way, the third stage achieves the lower siddhi.
All mantra methods are likewise explained in this manner.
This applies even when one is in the realm of a wicked king.
In places where there are many dangers from bandits,
among evil companions, or during times of famine and the like,
one should not dwell together with others to perform the rites of ritual purification.
Furthermore, there are three times during which the dharmas being cultivated and refined cannot be practiced;
one should discern and understand them well.
First, during times of extreme heat;
second, during times of torrential rain;
third, during times of extreme cold.
One does not cultivate the Great Dharma at this time;
rather, one cultivates the Dharma throughout the day.
Furthermore, there are three times during which one skillfully discerns and understands.
First, from the fifth watch until dawn;
second, from noon until the late afternoon;
third, from the seventh watch until the tenth watch of the night.
In this manner, during this time, the recitation and the performance of the ritual shall all be brought to completion.
Chapter Thirteen: The Ritual Altar for Homa. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of the Secret Traces, saying:
There are three secret dharmas that must be skillfully distinguished and understood.
If one does not understand and know the methods for recitation, then realization will not be achieved;
these are known as the fire altar (homa) rites.
The method for the furnace,
the method for consuming food while burning,
and these are called the three dharmas.
Each has its own three;
their natures are not identical.
If they were identical, then calamity and fault would arise.
When performing this *ābhicāruka* (subjugation) fire-offering in the hearth, one should not perform *puṣṭika* (nourishing) rites or *śāntika* (pacifying) rites. Why?
Because it is like placing bitter poison into sweet milk.
If milk is placed within [a vessel] containing poison, the milk will likewise become poisonous.
For this reason, three [fires] are prescribed for the śāntika fire altar.
The dimensions shall be four cubits or alternatively three cubits;
it should be smeared with clay according to the ritual rules.
In the center of the site, one should dig a circular pit for the hearth.
It is sixteen finger-breadths deep and twelve finger-breadths wide;
at the very bottom of the pit, one should further construct an earthen platform measuring four finger-breadths in height.
Furthermore, one may fashion upon the surface of the platform a wheel with twelve spokes, a rim, and hubs,
measuring one finger-breadth in height,
using clay mixed with white and yellow earth.
In accordance with the ritual, a clay furnace is prepared.
On the eastern gate of the maṇḍala, draw a golden wheel with twelve spokes;
on the southern gate, draw a trident.
On the western gate, draw the seal of the dragon;
on the northern gate, draw the seal of the vajra.
In each of the four corners, draw two vajras.
Form a cross.
On the first day of the waxing moon, bathe to become pure and don white, clean garments.
Eat only milk-rice, milk-gruel, and curd-gruel.
Having completely severed all discursive speech, the mind becomes pure, serene, and tranquil.
One recites within the altar until sunset;
then, facing south from the altar hearth, one spreads a mat of *māra* grass.
Sit facing north in a composed posture.
One should use agarwood, cypress wood, mulberry wood, or oak wood;
whichever of these woods is obtained may be used interchangeably.
Cut a piece of wood one span long with both ends even;
mix clarified butter and honey together and smear them on both ends;
recite the mantra over each one.
In the center of the hearth, stack the materials according to the ritual rules and ignite the fire.
Then, take equal portions of *nāga-keśara* (barley), large barley, small wheat, non-glutinous rice, and black sesame,
and mix each with clarified butter, milk, and curd.
Recite the mantra one thousand and eight times for each of the three periods of the day and burn [the incense] once during each period.
After completing seven days, or half a month, or a full month,
all karmic obstructions and all calamities shall be eliminated.
May merit, lifespan, and longevity increase, and may all things be peaceful and secure.
Furthermore, all ill-omened signs of malevolent stars and strange portents in the world shall likewise be dispersed and extinguished.
At night, when the sun has set, it is the time when the hosts of the Śuddhāvāsa deities descend to this realm to assemble;
they perform such rites in order to bring about the peaceful and secure dharma of the world.
Each time it is about to be used,
one should thoroughly rub and polish the furnace with a thin paste of pure white clay.
Regarding the pauṣṭika rite:
following the previous śāntika rite,
construct the altar and draw the mudrās.
Simply alter the furnace pit to be two cubits square and two cubits deep.
Within the pit, there shall be a circular earthen platform one cubit wide and four finger-breadths high.
One may fashion an eight-petaled lotus on the pedestal out of clay,
ensuring that both the pedestal and the petals of the flower are clearly defined. Then,
using red and yellow earth, one should apply a coating of clay according to the ritual rules.
On the first day of the waxing moon, purify the body and remain clean, don pure white garments,
consume the three white foods, and cease all idle conversation.
Recite the mantras within the mandala until sunrise.
Sit facing east on the western side of the altar and hearth,
seated upon a mat of *kuśa* grass with a heart of joy.
Use aloeswood, *guggulu*, mulberry wood, or cypress wood.
Cut it to a length of one span (vitasti), with both ends trimmed even.
Mix ghee, honey, milk, and curd together,
and dip each end [of the thread] into this mixture while reciting the mantra over each one.
Within the hearth, pile the materials according to the ritual rules and kindle the fire.
Use steamed non-glutinous rice and black sesame seeds in equal portions,
mixing them with ghee, honey, curd, and milk.
Recite the mantra once for each burning of the incense, repeating this one thousand and eight times.
Continue this for seven days, or half a month, or a full month.
By performing the ritual in this manner, one shall attain accomplishment, auspiciousness, abundance, and joy.
At this time of sunrise, when the auspicious devas descend to this world and assemble in joy,
one should practice the method for accomplishing happiness and seeking abundance in the world.
Performing the ritual in this manner,
whenever it is time [to begin], one should smear and wipe the furnace clean with pure red and yellow earth.
Furthermore, using *māra* wood, or *śrīveṣṭaka* (sandalwood) wood, or cypress wood,
one should cut them into pieces three times each day and kindle a fire.
Then, one should mix *guluñca* grass with saffron, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), honey, and so forth.
Roasting and boiling food for the *puṣṭika* rite,
one seeks great abundance and all manner of wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, one should completely cut pieces of *pāṭala* wood and ignite them as a fire;
then, having mixed black sesame, clarified butter, honey, and white mustard seeds together,
one should offer them as oblations into the sacrificial fire while reciting the mantra.
Furthermore, because one achieves three kinds of dharmas,
the *ḍākinī* rite is commenced on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
Alternatively, on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the dark fortnight,
wearing blue or red garments,
one should construct a triangular fire altar three cubits in size as an ornament.
Dig a pit one cubit deep;
let one corner point toward the east, one corner toward the west,
and one corner toward the south.
The upper rim of the altar should be three finger-widths wide,
and the height of the rim two finger-widths.
At the bottom of the pit, fashion a one-chi (one foot) three-pronged trident from clay,
measuring three finger-widths in height,
with the blade of its head pointing south.
Smear and wipe the entire area with black earth and mud.
At either midday or midnight,
stand facing north on the maṇḍala, placing the left foot upon the right.
Squatting with his body upright,
he furrowed his brow and stared with wide eyes, reciting mantras in a state of wrathful anger.
He used wood from the jujube tree and the *kṛtavedhana* tree.
One cubit in length, with a sharp head for cutting and slicing,
it is placed in a triangular hearth within the altar-pit.
Furthermore, one offers foul-smelling flowers, black mustard seeds, chaff, salt, human excrement, and *sattika-śa*.
Mix it with one's own *rudrākṣa* seeds;
recite the mantra once for each seed and burn them one thousand and eight times.
Do this separately at each session until three days or seven days have passed.
Then those obstructing malevolent spirits, ghosts, and the like will be unable to cause harm or affliction through physical ailments,
calamities, or pain in the limbs and joints, nor by causing the body’s destruction.
If one performs this rite for the sake of personally seeking wealth and treasures:
Then it will not be accomplished;
one shall instead fall back into the Avīci Hell.
For at the hour of noon and at midnight, it is the time when all evil yakṣas, rākṣasas, gods, and ghosts roam and assemble.
One who desires to accomplish all worldly methods for subduing others should perform the ritual in this manner;
whenever it is time to proceed, one should always use black earth and mud.
Wipe it all over with a cloth.
Lord Guhyapati, during the first, second, fourth, eighth, ninth, and twelfth months—
specifically from the first to the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) in these months— [one should perform this].
The first day of the month is auspicious for practicing and seeking the Great Dharma, which will certainly lead to accomplishment; however,
the first month of the year is a time of many obstacles.
Perform the superior and middling rites.
If signs corresponding to thunder and lightning appear,
you will certainly be free from obstacles and swiftly attain accomplishment.
In the second month, there is the danger of wind;
one should perform the rite for security when signs of a great wind appear.
In the fourth month, there is the danger of rain.
When performing the rite of subjugation, there will be signs of heavy rain;
during the eighth and ninth months, when there is neither cold nor heat,
there will be signs of difficulties such as thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts when performing the rite for abundance.
Only during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa (the twelfth month) is there a seeker of the Dharma free from all signs of obstacles;
such are these various obstacles.
These are all signs of supreme accomplishment.
These are the six periods of the bright fortnight,
from the first day to the fifteenth day.
One should cause them to practice the śāntika rite and the pauṣṭika rite,
so that all accomplishments and supreme aspirations may be fulfilled during these six dark fortnights.
From the first day to the fifteenth day,
one may also perform the pauṣṭika rite and the jīvitakara rite;
these are for all rites of accomplishment and the fulfillment of desired goals.
If these two dharmas are established and practiced according to the ritual during the lunar mansion of Bharaṇī or at the time of a lunar eclipse,
one will attain the supreme accomplishment.
Only during a solar eclipse may one perform the rites of accomplishment for the superior,
middling, and inferior levels. Such ritual procedures should all be performed on the first, third,
or fifth day of either the waxing or waning moon, or on the eighth day.
On either the thirteenth or fifteenth day,
one should perform the rites for the accomplishment of various substances.
If one is performing a rite of fierce accomplishment (*tīkṣṇa-sādhana*), [the procedure is as follows].
Furthermore, one should perform [the rite] during times when the *nakṣatras* and *grahas* are fierce,
or according to the characteristics of the three types of ritual methods (*karmapatha*).
As for the categories of these three types of ritual methods for accomplishment:
Each is to be performed as instructed in its respective ritual manual.
As for the time periods: the first and second months are the beginning of spring;
these are the initial seasons of the rains.
At this time, one should perform all the rites and dharmas of the superior and middle categories.
During the three or four months following [the end of winter], in the spring and summer seasons,
during the periods of the superior, medium, and inferior rains.
At this time, one should perform the *ṛtubaddha* rite.
During the fifth and sixth months, which are the hot season of summer,
it is the middle period of the rainy season.
Those who wish to achieve success should practice the rites for accomplishment during the lower period.
At the end of the seventh or eighth month, during the late summer or early autumn, following the rains and within the middle season,
one should perform the *śāntika* rite at that time.
At the end of the ninth and tenth months, at the beginning of autumn and winter,
and during the first period of winter, one should perform the *puṣṭika* rite.
This applies likewise to the seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
One should appropriately accomplish the three types of *siddhi*,
each distinguished into nine grades— superior, middling, and inferior.
There are three periods of the night.
When the first watch of the night has passed,
the appearance of the signs of the first watch constitutes the accomplishment of the lower stage.
At the middle time of the middle watch, [the signs appear].
When signs appear during the middle watch of the night, it is an intermediate accomplishment.
When the final watch of the night has arrived and signs appear during that time, it is a superior accomplishment.
During the first watch of the night,
this is the time for performing the *śāntika* rite;
during the middle watch of the night.
When performing the *abhicāruka* rite, it is during the latter part of the night;
when performing the *pauṣṭika* rite, it is likewise [during the middle part].

Thus, one should know the distinctions of these three times and nine grades, correlating them with their respective seasonal types and appropriate rites. These are the characteristics of the dharmas taught for these three periods, categorized as superior, middling, and inferior.
One should perform various ritual practices only during lunar or solar eclipses,
regardless of the specific time or season.
This applies particularly when one desires the rites for fierce accomplishments (*tīkṣṇa-siddhi*) or the rites of *abhicāruka* (subjugation).
During an eclipse of the sun or moon,
one who acts according to the Dharma attains the supreme correspondence.
In all cases where one wishes for a rite to succeed from its very commencement,
one should fast and remain silent for one, two, or three days.
This applies to the superior, middling, and inferior methods for cultivating *siddhi*.
Regarding the days corresponding to the lunar months within the twelve-month cycle,
one should know that from the first to the fifteenth day of each waxing moon,
one should perform the *śāntika* (pacifying), *pauṣṭika* (augmenting), and all rites for accomplishment and liberation.
From the first day to the fifteenth day of every dark fortnight, one should perform the *abhicāruka* rites for subjugation and suppression.
If there are calamities or disasters, one need not wait for these specific times; performing the rites according to the circumstances will likewise effect their averting and removal.
Guhyapati, when it is the proper time for performing the rites— whether superior, middling, or inferior—
and when it is not the proper time for performing them,
the mantra-practitioner who understands this well shall attain the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the three types of dharmas that manifest before one.
Therefore, Guhyapati,
if one is to be a mantra-practitioner who accomplishes the secret dharma of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin:
One should always maintain a fire using the wood of *vāyavya*, *śallakī*, *devadāru*, or *khadira*,
kindled with a sharp, level cut;
one should maintain it by offering *tila* seeds mixed with clarified butter, milk, and so forth.
If one performs the offering by burning incense at the three periods of each day,
the mantra-deities will be pleased and provide protection,
granting the three *siddhis*.
Guhya-pati, those who thus attain the three siddhis do so by means of body,
speech, and mind that are of the nature of the dharmadhātu—
unchanging and immovable in suchness— as they cultivate the vinaya-dharma and recite the dharma-fire rites.
Then one attains the realization of the three kinds of siddhi:
first, celestial siddhi;
second, space siddhi.
Third is the *siddhi* of the stages (*bhūmi*).
This realizes the third stage;
according to whether the practiced methods are superior, middling, or inferior, one obtains the dharma, vows, and wealth.
Guhyapati, if you wish to accomplish all mantra-dharmas,
you should give rise to right view and compassion for all beings,
make offerings to all Buddhas, and not dwell in worldly dharmas.
If one seeking the unsurpassed path focuses one's efforts on sealing stūpas,
one will swiftly achieve accomplishment and realize the three stages.
In this present life, one’s merit and virtue will increase and reach fulfillment;
in whatever place one is born hereafter, one shall constantly experience blessings and happiness.
Furthermore, Guhyapati, this is the King of Mantras.
All those past Tathāgatas— immeasurable and innumerable, bearing both identical and different names—
who were all once ordinary beings,
likewise attained this supreme bodhi-samādhi dharma of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King Mantra.
I have attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
I, too, have realized and perfected this supreme samādhi dharma of the One-Syllable Cūḍāmaṇi King of Mantras for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi;
I have attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, once again observing with his Buddha-eye all the infinite and boundless Buddha-fields,
earnestly addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi three times, saying:
The rules, established rites, ritual procedures, firm dharmas, fruition dharmas, mandala dharmas,
and fire dharmas taught in my other mantra sections may all be adopted as appropriate within this dharma.
This is the method for the accomplishment of the Mañjuśrī-Vajra Family,
as well as the methods for the Buddha Family, the Avalokiteśvara Family, and the Vajragarbha Bodhisattva Family, which explain the mudrās and mantras.
One may employ them all as desired;
by the power of those mantras, the vināyakas will be unable to obstruct or afflict.
This is the seal-dharma of Bhṛkuṭī from the Vajra family.
One may also select and employ [mantras] from this section as appropriate.
Therefore, O Lord of Secrets, a practitioner of mantras should never consume onions, garlic, leeks, oil, radishes, earth-fertilizers, or similar foods.
Food that is foul-smelling to the world, or food that has been defiled by impurities—none of these should be eaten.
If one eats such things, one will not realize the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*) or the efficacy of the rites.
Such teachings as these have been briefly explained here.
If I were to dwell for an eon expounding and explaining it in detail, even within that small portion it would not be exhausted. Why is this?
Because it is the place where I originally realized and attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, this is the place where all Tathāgatas of the past realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For this reason, Guhyapati, [I have dispatched] the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and so forth.
Abiding for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas,
I have taught this dharma of the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin Samādhi through various skillful means; yet even this is but a small portion,
and it is not exhaustive.
If there should be someone who attains this King of Dharmas, the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣacakravartin,
and practices, upholds, recites, and reverently makes offerings to it according to the Dharma,
from this life until the attainment of Bodhi.
They shall not regress further.
It should be known that such persons have already, in the past, accumulated the provisions and the roots of merit for awakening.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, [they do not regress].
Therefore, at this time, one attains the complete and perfect Dharma-king of the One-Syllable Cakravartin.
Then, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of the Secret, and all the great bodhisattvas—
The great assembly of bhikṣus, along with devas, mantra-reciting seers, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
And all those in the world, both humans and non-humans alike,
having heard the Buddha preach this sutra at that time,
were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Scripture of the One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin, Scroll Five.
